lessons.plain: Laptops pack their parts tightly, so replacing one means working in a careful order instead of just pulling things out. The four parts here are the most commonly swapped: the battery (stored power), the keyboard, the touchpad (the flat pad you slide a finger on to move the pointer), and the internal wireless card (a small board that gives the laptop Wi-Fi and often Bluetooth). Think of it like changing a car part: you disconnect the power first, follow the maker's repair guide, keep track of every screw and cable, and test before closing everything up.
lessons.guessPrompt: You are about to replace the Wi-Fi card inside a laptop. Before touching any internal part, what do you think you should disconnect first, and why?
lessons.teach:
Replacing laptop hardware means swapping a field-replaceable unit (FRU, a part designed to be changed by a technician) using a safe, repeatable order. Start with the service manual, the manufacturer's repair guide showing screw locations and removal steps, because every model differs. Power off, unplug the charger, and disconnect the battery. Many modern batteries are internal, held by screws with a cable to the motherboard; older ones slide out from outside. Wear an ESD strap (a wrist strap that drains electrostatic discharge, the static spark that can silently damage chips) clipped to bare metal.

The keyboard and touchpad usually connect through ribbon cables, thin flat cables that slide into ZIF connectors (zero insertion force: you lift a small latch, the cable slides in, you close the latch). Some keyboards come out from the top after releasing clips; others are riveted to the palm-rest and the whole top case is replaced.

The wireless card is normally an M.2 card, a small slotted board held by one screw. Two or more thin antenna leads snap onto tiny round connectors on it; the antennas themselves run up into the screen lid.

Worked example, Wi-Fi card swap: one, shut down, unplug, remove the bottom panel. Two, disconnect the battery cable. Three, note which antenna lead goes on which connector (often labelled main and aux, or 1 and 2), then gently pry them straight up. Four, remove the screw; the card pops up at an angle; slide it out. Five, insert the new card at the same angle, press down, replace the screw. Six, reattach both antennas to the matching connectors. Seven, reconnect the battery, boot, install the driver, and confirm Wi-Fi works before refitting the panel.

A common mistake is forgetting or swapping the antenna leads. The laptop may still connect, but with weak signal and frequent drops, which users report as a Wi-Fi problem days later. Skipping the battery disconnect risks shorting the board. Sort screws by location, because a long screw in a short hole can pierce the board.

questions.prompt: A technician at a print shop is replacing the touchpad on a laptop whose internal battery is screwed in place. Here is the job so far. Step 1: open the service manual for this exact model to find screw locations. Step 2: power off, unplug the charger, clip an ESD strap to bare metal, and remove the bottom panel. Step 3: disconnect the battery cable from the motherboard. Step 4: (missing) free the touchpad's thin flat ribbon cable from its ZIF connector. Step 5: remove the touchpad screws, keep them in a tray sorted by location, and lift the old touchpad out. Step 6: seat the new touchpad, slide its ribbon cable into the connector, and close the latch. Step 7: reconnect the battery, boot, and test the touchpad before refitting the panel. What is Step 4?
choices: Lift the small latch on the ZIF connector, then gently slide the ribbon cable out
Unscrew the connector from the motherboard and remove it together with the ribbon cable
Pull the ribbon cable straight out with the latch left closed, since zero insertion force means it slides free on its own
Pry the cable end straight up off its small round connector, the same way you would lift an antenna lead
questions.why: A ZIF connector holds the ribbon cable with a latch, so you open the latch first and then the cable slides out without force, matching how Step 6 closes it again.

questions.prompt: A new hire at a regional bank's IT desk asks what a ZIF connector is. Which answer is correct?
choices: A tiny round connector that an antenna lead snaps onto and pries straight off
A part designed to be swapped out by a technician rather than repaired
A connector where you lift a small latch, slide the ribbon cable in, then close the latch to hold it
A slotted connector that holds a small board at an angle until a single screw presses it down
questions.why: ZIF stands for zero insertion force: the latch is opened, the ribbon cable goes in without pushing, and closing the latch locks it.

questions.prompt: At a veterinary clinic, a technician replaced a laptop's M.2 wireless card on Monday. It connected to Wi-Fi fine during the test. On Thursday the user reports weak signal and frequent drops, though other laptops in the same room work normally. What is the most likely cause to check first?
choices: The new card's driver was never installed, so the card cannot work
The battery was left disconnected, so the card is underpowered
The card's screw is too long and has pierced the motherboard
The two antenna leads were swapped or one was left off the card
questions.why: Swapped or missing antenna leads typically still allow a connection but cause weak signal and drops that users report days later.

questions.prompt: A technician at a logistics company removes eight screws from a laptop's bottom panel and internal parts, drops them all into one cup, and later fits them back in whatever holes they happen to suit. What is the main risk the teaching text warns about?
choices: Static from the screws can silently damage the chips
The keyboard's riveted top case will need to be replaced
A long screw driven into a short hole can pierce the motherboard
The battery may short the board because it was not disconnected
questions.why: Screws differ in length by location, and putting a long screw where a short one belongs can push through and damage the board, which is why you sort them by location.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the safe order for replacing a laptop's internal Wi-Fi card or keyboard, and name one tradeoff or limit of doing this kind of repair on a modern laptop.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I find the service manual for that exact model, because screw locations and removal order change between models. I shut down, unplug the charger, put on an ESD strap, open the bottom panel, and disconnect the battery before touching anything else so nothing gets shorted. For a Wi-Fi card I note which antenna lead goes where, unclip them, remove the one screw, swap the M.2 card and reattach the leads correctly, otherwise signal will be weak. For a keyboard I open the ZIF latch to free the ribbon cable rather than yanking it. I keep screws sorted by location, then reconnect the battery and test before closing up. The limit is that many modern laptops have glued or riveted parts, so a keyboard swap may mean replacing the whole top case, which costs more time and money.
rubricPoints: Consult the model's service manual before opening the laptop.
Power off, unplug, and disconnect the battery before working inside.
Use ESD protection to avoid static damage.
Handle ribbon cables through ZIF latches and reconnect Wi-Fi antenna leads to the correct connectors.
Test the device before fully reassembling it.
Name a limit, such as riveted keyboards requiring a whole top-case replacement.

suggested.rationale: This is a physical procedure and safe ordering of steps, and no current mission or planned engine simulates opening laptop hardware, so careful reading of the sequence fits best.

lessons.plain: Many laptops let you add or swap two internal parts to make them faster or roomier: memory sticks and a small storage card. Laptop memory comes as a short stick called a SODIMM, and fast storage often comes as a thin card called an M.2 drive. Upgrading is mostly a matching game, like buying a replacement bulb: it has to fit the socket and speak the same electrical language, or it either won't go in or won't work. Before you buy anything, check what the laptop actually supports, because some laptops have parts soldered down that can't be changed at all.
lessons.guessPrompt: A friend buys a memory stick from a desktop computer and wants to put it in their laptop. Do you think it will fit, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A SODIMM (small outline dual inline memory module) is the short memory stick laptops use, about half the length of a desktop DIMM, so the two are not interchangeable. Memory also comes in generations, DDR4 and DDR5 being the common ones today (DDR means double data rate). Each generation has its notch, a small gap in the gold contacts, in a different place, so the wrong generation physically will not seat. Speed ratings matter less: faster memory usually runs at the slower speed the laptop supports. Installing two matched sticks can enable dual channel, where the processor reads both sticks at once for more bandwidth.

M.2 is a form factor, meaning a physical shape and connector, not a speed. An M.2 card is described by a size code such as 2280 (22 mm wide, 80 mm long) and a key, the notch pattern on its connector. An M.2 drive can use one of two protocols, meaning the language it speaks: older SATA, or NVMe (non-volatile memory express), which runs over PCIe lanes and is several times faster. NVMe drives are typically M-key; SATA M.2 drives are often B+M key.

Worked example: a laptop's manual lists DDR4 SODIMM, 2 slots, max 32 GB, and one M.2 2280 slot supporting NVMe PCIe. Step one, buy DDR4 SODIMMs, not DDR5 or desktop sticks. Step two, total no more than 32 GB, so two 16 GB sticks. Step three, pick a 2280 NVMe drive. Step four, power off, unplug, disconnect the battery if possible, wear an anti-static wrist strap to avoid electrostatic discharge damage, insert at an angle, press down, and secure.

Common mistake: assuming every M.2 slot accepts NVMe. A slot wired only for SATA may fit an NVMe card physically yet never detect it, so the drive simply doesn't appear in firmware. Likewise, many thin laptops have RAM soldered to the board, so it cannot be upgraded at all. Always confirm against the manufacturer's specifications before buying.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic's laptop manual lists: DDR5 SODIMM, 2 slots, max 64 GB; one M.2 2242 slot supporting SATA only. The technician plans the upgrade. Step one: buy DDR5 SODIMMs, not DDR4 or desktop DIMMs. Step two: buy two matched 32 GB sticks, totalling 64 GB and enabling dual channel. Step three: ______. Step four: power off, unplug, disconnect the battery if possible, wear an anti-static wrist strap, insert each part at an angle, press down, and secure. Which choice correctly completes step three?
choices: Buy a 2242 M.2 drive that uses the SATA protocol
Buy any M.2 drive, because M.2 is a speed rating that guarantees compatibility
Buy a 2280 SATA M.2 drive, because only the protocol has to match the slot
Buy a 2242 NVMe drive, because NVMe is faster and any M.2 slot will accept it
questions.why: The slot accepts only 2242-sized cards that speak SATA, so the drive must match both the size code and the protocol.

questions.prompt: A coworker says, "This drive is M.2, so it must be the fast kind." What does the term M.2 actually describe?
choices: The protocol the drive uses to talk to the computer
A guaranteed minimum transfer speed
A physical shape and connector, known as a form factor
The memory generation the drive is compatible with
questions.why: M.2 names a form factor, which is the physical shape and connector. The drive's speed depends on its protocol, which can be SATA or NVMe.

questions.prompt: A laptop's specifications support DDR4 SODIMM memory rated at 2666. A technician installs a matched pair of DDR4 SODIMMs rated at 3200. What is the most likely result?
choices: The laptop will run the memory at 3200 and gain extra speed
The sticks will not seat, because the notch differs between speed ratings
The memory will work but run at the slower 2666 speed the laptop supports
The laptop will refuse to start until slower memory is installed
questions.why: Speed ratings matter less than the generation. Faster memory of the correct generation usually runs at the slower speed the laptop supports.

questions.prompt: A technician installs a new M.2 NVMe drive in a laptop. The card fits the slot and screws down normally, but the drive never appears in the firmware. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The laptop has soldered RAM, which blocks storage upgrades
The drive needs a desktop DIMM slot to be recognised
The slot is wired only for SATA, so it cannot detect an NVMe drive
The drive's size code is wrong, since an incorrect size always fails silently
questions.why: An NVMe card can physically fit a slot that is wired only for SATA, yet the drive is never detected. That is why the slot's supported protocol must be confirmed before buying.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose RAM and an M.2 drive for a customer's laptop upgrade, and name one limit that could stop the upgrade even if the part physically fits.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I look up the laptop's specs. For memory I need SODIMM, not desktop DIMM, in the right generation, like DDR4 or DDR5; the notch differs so the wrong one won't seat. I also check the slot count and maximum supported capacity, and I'd buy matched pairs so it can run dual channel. For storage, M.2 is just the shape, so I check the length code like 2280, the key, and which protocol the slot supports, SATA or NVMe over PCIe. The big trap is that an NVMe drive can physically fit a SATA-only M.2 slot and then never be detected. Another limit is soldered RAM on thin laptops, which can't be upgraded at all. During install I power down, disconnect the battery and use ESD protection.
rubricPoints: Laptops use SODIMM memory, which differs from desktop DIMMs.
RAM generation (DDR4 vs DDR5) must match and is enforced by the notch position.
Check slot count and maximum supported memory capacity.
M.2 is a form factor; check size code, key, and SATA versus NVMe support.
Names a limit such as a SATA-only M.2 slot or soldered RAM.
Mentions safe install practice like power off, battery disconnect, and ESD protection.

suggested.rationale: No current mission involves physical hardware, so reasoning through exam-style compatibility scenarios best builds the matching skill the exam tests.

lessons.plain: Phones, tablets and laptops connect to extra gear called accessories: chargers, headphones, keyboards, monitors and payment terminals. They connect in two ways. Wired ports, such as USB-C or Apple's Lightning, carry power and data through a plug. Wireless links, such as Bluetooth and NFC, use short-range radio instead of a cable. A docking station is a hub that gives a laptop power, screens, network and peripherals through a single connection. Think of a dock like a power strip for everything at your desk: plug in one thing and the whole workspace comes alive. Configuring accessories means matching the right port, cable and settings so each one works.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user plugs a monitor into their laptop's USB-C port using a cheap USB-C cable that came with a phone charger, and the screen stays black. Before any teaching, what do you think might be wrong?
lessons.teach:
USB-C is a small, reversible connector. It can carry data, charging power through USB Power Delivery (a standard that lets the device and charger agree on higher wattage), and video through alternate mode, which sends a display signal such as DisplayPort over the same plug. Thunderbolt is a faster standard that uses the USB-C shape and is usually marked with a lightning-bolt icon. Lightning is Apple's own reversible connector, used on older iPhones and iPads. Newer iPhones moved to USB-C.

The key fact is that a USB-C plug shape promises nothing about features. A port may lack video support. A cable may be charge-only or limited to slow USB 2.0 speeds. Always check the port markings and the cable rating.

Bluetooth is short-range radio, typically about 10 meters, for headsets, keyboards and mice. Pairing is the one-time introduction between two devices. You turn Bluetooth on, put the accessory into pairing or discoverable mode, select it on the phone or laptop, and confirm a matching PIN or passkey if one is asked. After that the two devices remember each other and reconnect automatically.

NFC, or near-field communication, works only within a few centimeters. It is used for tap-to-pay, building badges, and quick tap-to-pair with some speakers.

A docking station connects a laptop to monitors, wired network, USB devices and power through one cable or slot. A simpler version without its own power or extra features is called a port replicator.

Worked example: monitors on a USB-C dock stay black. First, confirm the laptop port supports video or Thunderbolt. Second, check that the dock has its own power adapter plugged in. Third, swap in the cable that came with the dock. Fourth, update the dock firmware and the display drivers. In this example, the cable swap fixes it.

A common mistake is assuming every USB-C cable and port is equal. The result in the field is slow charging, missing video, and wasted hardware replacements.

questions.prompt: At a dental clinic, a front-desk tablet with a USB-C port charges very slowly from a new 65-watt USB-C charger. The technician works through it. Step 1: She confirms the charger supports USB Power Delivery, so the tablet and charger can agree on a higher wattage. Step 2: She confirms the tablet's USB-C port is the one meant for charging. Step 3: ??? Step 4: She retests, and the tablet now charges at full speed. Which action is the missing Step 3?
choices: Replace the tablet's battery, since slow charging means the battery is worn out
Turn on NFC so the tablet can negotiate power with the charger
Swap the thin, unmarked USB-C cable for one rated for the charger's wattage
Put the tablet into Bluetooth discoverable mode and pair it with the charger
questions.why: A USB-C plug shape promises nothing about features, so an unrated or charge-limited cable can slow charging even when the charger and port both support higher wattage.

questions.prompt: A design studio buys a small box that connects to a laptop through one cable. It adds a few USB ports and a network jack, but it has no power adapter of its own and no extra features. What is this simpler device called?
choices: An alternate mode adapter
A Lightning hub
A Thunderbolt dock
A port replicator
questions.why: A port replicator is a simpler version of a docking station that has no power supply of its own and no extra features.

questions.prompt: A call-center agent gets a new Bluetooth headset. Bluetooth is turned on in the laptop's settings, but the headset never shows up in the list of devices to select. What should the agent do next?
choices: Move the headset at least 10 meters away so the signal is not overloaded
Put the headset into pairing or discoverable mode so the laptop can find it
Tap the headset against the laptop so NFC can complete the pairing
Plug the headset into the laptop with a USB-C cable to update its firmware
questions.why: Pairing requires the accessory to be in pairing or discoverable mode before the laptop can see it and select it.

questions.prompt: An accountant plugs a USB-C monitor cable into the only USB-C port on her laptop. The monitor shows no signal. The port has no lightning-bolt icon and no display marking. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The laptop's port may not support video, because a USB-C plug shape does not guarantee features
USB-C cannot carry video, so the monitor needs a Lightning connector instead
The laptop needs USB Power Delivery turned off before it can send video
The monitor must be paired with Bluetooth before USB-C video will work
questions.why: A USB-C port only carries video if it supports alternate mode or Thunderbolt, and the plug shape alone does not tell you that, so the port markings matter.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would get a new Bluetooth headset and a USB-C docking station working for a user, and name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: For the headset, I'd turn Bluetooth on in the laptop's settings and hold the headset's button until it enters pairing mode. Then I'd pick it from the device list and confirm the PIN if one appears. After that one-time pairing, the two devices remember each other. The limit is range: Bluetooth usually reaches about 10 meters, and walls or interference cut that down. Each accessory also has to be paired once per host. For the dock, I'd first check that the laptop's USB-C port supports video or Thunderbolt, since not every USB-C port does. I'd plug in the dock's own power adapter and use the cable that came with it, because some USB-C cables are charge-only or slow. Then I'd update the dock firmware and drivers. The tradeoff is convenience versus compatibility: one cable is easy, but only when the port, cable and dock all support the same features.
rubricPoints: Describes Bluetooth pairing steps: enable, pairing mode, select, confirm PIN.
Notes Bluetooth's short range of about 10 meters.
States that USB-C ports and cables differ in video, power and speed support.
Checks dock power, cable and firmware or drivers when troubleshooting.
Names a real tradeoff or limit for each accessory.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine covers physical accessories, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios like a dark dock monitor or a headset that won't pair builds the needed judgment best.

lessons.plain: A phone or tablet can reach the internet and other devices in a few different ways, and each one is a separate radio you can switch on or off. Wi-Fi connects to a nearby wireless network, like a home router. Cellular data uses the phone carrier's towers, so it works almost anywhere with signal. A hotspot or tethering lets the phone share its own internet with a laptop. Airplane mode turns all the radios off at once. Think of a house with several doors: each door is a different way in, and airplane mode locks every door with one key.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user says their phone shows full Wi-Fi bars at the office but nothing loads, and when they walk outside to the car park, web pages suddenly work again. What do you think is different between the two places?
lessons.teach:
Mobile network connectivity means the set of radios and settings a phone or tablet uses to send and receive data. Wi-Fi is short-range wireless networking to an access point (the box that broadcasts the network name, called the SSID). Joining needs the correct SSID and, usually, a password using a security standard such as WPA2 or WPA3. Cellular data is internet service from a mobile carrier over its towers, using generations like 4G LTE or 5G, and needs an active plan and a SIM (a small card or built-in eSIM that identifies the subscriber). Tethering shares the phone's cellular connection with another device over USB or Bluetooth. A hotspot shares it over Wi-Fi, so the phone acts as a small access point with its own SSID and password. Airplane mode disables all transmitting radios. On most modern devices you can then switch Wi-Fi and Bluetooth back on individually while cellular stays off.

It works because the operating system usually prefers Wi-Fi over cellular to save the data plan. Worked example: a user's phone shows Wi-Fi connected but nothing loads. Step 1, check that airplane mode is off and Wi-Fi is on. Both are true. Step 2, turn Wi-Fi off. The phone falls back to cellular and pages load, so the phone itself is fine. Step 3, the fault is on the Wi-Fi side, such as a guest network that needs a sign-in page or a router with no internet. Step 4, forget the network, rejoin it, and complete any sign-in page.

A common mistake is assuming signal bars mean internet. Bars show a radio link to the access point or tower, not a working path to the internet. Another mistake is leaving airplane mode on after a flight. The user then reports that everything is broken, and the fix is simply to toggle it off. Hotspot use also drains the battery fast and consumes plan data, and some carriers block or limit it. When troubleshooting, change one radio at a time so you know which connection is actually at fault.

questions.prompt: A surveyor at a rural job site needs her laptop online to upload 40 site photos. There is no Wi-Fi nearby, but her phone has 5G service and an active data plan. Step 1: she confirms airplane mode is off on the phone and that cellular data loads a web page. Step 2: she turns on the phone's hotspot and notes the network name (SSID) and password it shows. Step 3: ??? Step 4: the laptop opens a web page and the upload starts. She also plugs the phone into a charger, because sharing a connection drains the battery quickly. What is Step 3?
choices: Remove the SIM card from the phone and insert it into the laptop so the laptop can reach the carrier.
Pair the laptop with the phone over Bluetooth, then type the password of her office Wi-Fi network.
On the phone, turn on airplane mode so the hotspot gets all of the phone's radio power.
On the laptop, pick the phone's hotspot SSID from the list of Wi-Fi networks and enter the hotspot password.
questions.why: A hotspot makes the phone act as a small access point with its own SSID and password, so the laptop joins it like any other Wi-Fi network, while airplane mode would cut the cellular link being shared.

questions.prompt: A sales rep wants to share his phone's cellular internet with his laptop. Which statement correctly tells tethering apart from a hotspot?
choices: Tethering shares the connection over Wi-Fi, while a hotspot shares it over USB or Bluetooth.
Tethering needs a SIM card, while a hotspot works without any carrier plan.
Tethering shares an existing Wi-Fi connection, while a hotspot shares the cellular connection.
Tethering shares the connection over USB or Bluetooth, while a hotspot shares it over Wi-Fi with its own SSID and password.
questions.why: Both share the phone's cellular data, but tethering uses a USB cable or Bluetooth, and a hotspot uses Wi-Fi, with the phone acting as a small access point.

questions.prompt: During a three-hour flight, a passenger has switched on airplane mode on her modern phone. She wants to listen to music on her wireless Bluetooth earbuds without turning cellular back on. What should she do?
choices: Start the phone's hotspot so the earbuds can connect to it as a Wi-Fi network.
Leave airplane mode on and switch Bluetooth back on by itself; cellular stays off.
Remove the SIM card, which turns Bluetooth back on automatically.
Turn airplane mode off, because Bluetooth cannot work while airplane mode is enabled.
questions.why: Airplane mode disables all transmitting radios, but on most modern devices Wi-Fi and Bluetooth can then be re-enabled individually while cellular remains off.

questions.prompt: A delivery driver's tablet shows full cellular signal bars with the 4G LTE icon, yet no app can load data. What can a technician correctly conclude from the full bars alone?
choices: The tablet has a radio link to the tower, but that does not prove a working path to the internet, so the plan, SIM, or carrier side still need checking.
The tablet's internet connection is working, so the fault must be inside the apps themselves.
Airplane mode must be on, because full bars only appear when airplane mode is enabled.
The tablet must be connected to Wi-Fi, because cellular never shows signal bars.
questions.why: Signal bars only show a radio link to the tower or access point, not a working internet path, so items like an active plan and SIM still need checking.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Wi-Fi, cellular data, tethering/hotspot and airplane mode relate on a phone, and name one limit or tradeoff of using a hotspot.
lessons.modelAnswer: A phone has separate radios. Wi-Fi joins a local access point by its SSID and password. Cellular data uses the carrier's towers and needs a SIM or eSIM and an active plan. The phone normally prefers Wi-Fi, so when Wi-Fi is up but broken, pages fail even though cellular would work. Tethering shares the phone's cellular connection with another device over USB or Bluetooth, and a hotspot does the same over Wi-Fi with its own network name. Airplane mode turns every radio off. You can usually re-enable Wi-Fi or Bluetooth on their own afterwards. To troubleshoot, toggle one radio at a time to isolate the faulty path, and remember that signal bars don't prove internet access. The tradeoff with a hotspot is that it drains the battery quickly and uses plan data, and some carriers restrict it.
rubricPoints: Wi-Fi needs the correct SSID and password, while cellular needs a SIM or eSIM and an active plan.
Phones usually prefer Wi-Fi, so a broken Wi-Fi network can block access even when cellular works.
Tethering uses USB or Bluetooth, while a hotspot shares the cellular connection over Wi-Fi.
Airplane mode disables all radios, and Wi-Fi or Bluetooth can be re-enabled individually.
Signal bars show a radio link, not proof of working internet access.
Names a hotspot tradeoff such as battery drain, data use or carrier limits.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or engine covers mobile radios, so reasoning through exam-style 'phone can't connect' scenarios best builds the skill of isolating which connection is at fault.

lessons.plain: Syncing means keeping the same information, such as contacts, calendars, email, photos and files, matching on a phone and somewhere else, either a computer connected by cable or Wi-Fi, or an online account (the cloud). Change a contact on one and the other updates. Mobile device management (MDM) is how a company remotely controls work phones and tablets. It sends the device a profile, a bundle of settings and rules like a required passcode, the office Wi-Fi and the work email account. Think of syncing as a shared notebook that stays identical in two places, and an MDM profile as the employee handbook a new hire must accept on day one.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new employee loses their company phone on a train. Without ever touching the phone again, how do you think the IT team could protect the work email and files stored on it?
lessons.teach:
Synchronization (sync) is the two-way process that keeps data identical on a mobile device and another location. Cloud sync uses an online account, such as an Apple ID, Google account or Microsoft 365 account, so data flows over any internet connection, usually in the background. Desktop sync uses a cable or local Wi-Fi connection to a computer running companion software, which is useful for offline backups or large media libraries. Commonly synced items are contacts, calendars, email, photos, bookmarks, documents and app data. Sync works because each side tracks what changed and when, then copies the newer version across. When both sides change the same item before syncing, a sync conflict occurs, and the software must keep one version or both copies.

Mobile device management (MDM) is a central service that IT uses to configure and control many devices. Enrollment is the step that registers a device with the MDM server. After enrollment, the server pushes a configuration profile, a signed package of settings such as passcode rules, Wi-Fi credentials, VPN (an encrypted tunnel into the company network), email accounts and certificates, plus restrictions like blocking the camera. MDM can also remotely lock or wipe a lost device. BYOD (bring your own device) means staff use personal phones, so companies often separate work data from personal data and wipe only the work portion.

Worked example: Priya enrolls her new company phone. First, she signs in and accepts the profile. Second, the phone receives the office Wi-Fi and email automatically. Third, it is forced to set a six-digit passcode. Fourth, her work calendar syncs from the cloud. A month later the phone is stolen, and IT sends a remote wipe.

A common mistake is treating sync as a backup. Sync copies deletions too, so a contact deleted by mistake on the phone also vanishes from the cloud. Another mistake is removing an MDM profile to fix a setting. Doing that strips the work email, Wi-Fi and VPN it supplied, and the user loses access until the device is enrolled again.

questions.prompt: Diego is a delivery driver for a bakery chain, and IT gives him a new tablet. Step 1: Diego signs in with his work account, which registers the tablet with the company's MDM server (enrollment). Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: Without Diego typing anything, the tablet now joins the depot Wi-Fi, connects to the company VPN, and has its camera blocked. Step 4: The tablet forces him to set a passcode before he can continue. Which choice best fills Step 2?
choices: Diego plugs the tablet into a depot computer so companion software can sync his contacts over the cable
Diego copies the Wi-Fi password and VPN details from a printed sheet into the tablet's settings
The MDM server pushes a signed configuration profile containing the Wi-Fi, VPN, passcode and restriction settings, and Diego accepts it
IT sends a remote wipe so the tablet starts from a clean state before setup
questions.why: After enrollment, the MDM server delivers a configuration profile, and that profile is what applies the Wi-Fi, VPN, passcode rules and camera restriction automatically.

questions.prompt: At a law office, Amara edits a client meeting's time in her phone's calendar while offline. Before her phone reconnects, a colleague changes the same meeting in the shared cloud calendar. When the phone syncs, what situation has occurred?
choices: A normal one-way backup, because the cloud copy always overwrites whatever is on the phone
A sync conflict, because both sides changed the same item before syncing, so the software must keep one version or both copies
A failed enrollment, because the phone is no longer registered with the MDM server
A remote wipe, because the cloud account detected two different versions of the data
questions.why: A sync conflict happens when both sides change the same item before syncing, and the sync software then has to keep one version or both copies.

questions.prompt: A design studio lets staff use their own personal phones for work email and files. One employee reports her personal phone lost. What is the most appropriate MDM action that respects this arrangement?
choices: Fully wipe the whole phone, including her personal photos and apps
Remove her cloud account password so the phone can no longer sync anything
Do nothing, because MDM cannot act on a phone the company does not own
Remotely wipe only the work portion of the phone, leaving her personal data alone
questions.why: Under BYOD (bring your own device), companies separate work data from personal data so they can wipe just the work portion of a lost personal phone.

questions.prompt: At a veterinary clinic, a technician's phone has a wrong setting that came from the clinic's MDM configuration profile. To fix it quickly, he deletes the profile from the phone. What is the most likely result?
choices: He loses the work email, Wi-Fi and VPN the profile supplied until the phone is enrolled again
His personal photos and contacts are erased because the phone performs a remote wipe
Nothing changes, because profile settings are stored in the cloud account rather than on the phone
Only the incorrect setting is removed, and all other work settings stay in place
questions.why: Removing an MDM profile strips everything it supplied, such as work email, Wi-Fi and VPN, so the user loses access until the device is re-enrolled.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between syncing a phone and enrolling it in MDM, and name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: Syncing keeps the same data, such as contacts, calendars, email and photos, matching between a phone and either a computer or a cloud account. Each side notes what changed and copies the newer version over. MDM is different. It is IT registering the phone with a central server and pushing a configuration profile with settings like the required passcode, Wi-Fi, VPN and work email, plus restrictions and the ability to lock or wipe the phone remotely. One limit of sync is that it is not a backup, because deletions and mistakes copy across too. Conflicts can also happen when both sides change the same item. A tradeoff of MDM is control versus privacy. On personal BYOD phones, users may resist full control, so companies often manage and wipe only the work data. Also, removing the profile removes everything it supplied.
rubricPoints: Defines sync as keeping data matched between a device and a computer or cloud account.
Defines MDM as central management that enrolls devices and pushes configuration profiles.
Gives examples of profile contents such as passcode rules, Wi-Fi, VPN, email or restrictions.
Notes that sync is not a backup because deletions propagate, or mentions sync conflicts.
Names an MDM tradeoff such as BYOD privacy, separating work data, or losing access when a profile is removed.
Mentions remote lock or wipe as a protection for lost devices.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine covers mobile sync or MDM, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about lost devices, BYOD and failed sync builds the judgment the exam tests.

lessons.plain: Phones, tablets and laptops have a few physical parts that commonly misbehave: the battery, which stores charge; the cooling, which keeps the device from getting too hot; and the digitizer, the clear touch-sensing layer over the screen that turns your finger into a location. Troubleshooting means working from the symptom back to the likely cause and checking the cheapest, easiest things first. A mechanic checks tire pressure before replacing the engine. Short battery life might mean an aging battery or an app that drains power. Heat might come from blocked vents or a heavy workload. Dead touch might be a dirty screen, a bad screen protector, or a cracked layer.
lessons.guessPrompt: A two-year-old phone that used to last all day now dies by mid-afternoon, and nothing else seems wrong. Before buying any part, what two things would you check first?
lessons.teach:
Three hardware symptoms show up constantly on mobile devices.

Short battery life means the device runs out of charge much faster than it used to. Nearly all phones and laptops use lithium-ion batteries, a rechargeable type that loses capacity with every charge cycle. One charge cycle is one full 0 to 100 percent of use, which may be spread across several partial charges. After a few hundred cycles, the battery holds noticeably less. Check two things: the built-in battery health report, and the list of power use per app. If one app or setting is draining power, such as high screen brightness or constant location tracking, fix that. If health is low, replace the battery. A swollen battery bulges and can lift the case or screen. Take it out of service at once, and never charge it or press on it, because it can catch fire.

Overheating means the device gets hot enough to slow down or shut off. Devices protect themselves with thermal throttling, which deliberately lowers processor speed to cut heat. Common causes are blocked vents (a laptop on a blanket), dust in the fan, heavy apps, direct sun, charging while gaming, or dried thermal paste. Thermal paste is the compound that carries heat from the chip to the heatsink.

An unresponsive digitizer ignores touches or registers them in the wrong place. Possible causes are dirt or moisture, a thick or bubbled screen protector, a case pressing on the edges, a frozen operating system, or bad calibration. Calibration is the mapping between where you touch and where the screen thinks you touched. Physical causes include cracked glass or a loose internal cable.

Worked example: a tablet ignores touches along the bottom inch of the screen. Step one: clean the screen and dry your hands. Still dead. Step two: remove the case and the protector. Still dead. Step three: restart the tablet. Still dead. Step four: run calibration or a touch test. The strip registers nothing, yet the picture looks fine. Conclusion: the digitizer is damaged, so replace the digitizer or screen assembly, not the display alone.

The common mistake is replacing parts before ruling out cheap causes such as a protector, an app, or a blocked vent. That wastes money. Ignoring a swollen battery or constant heat can lead to data loss, a dead motherboard, or a fire.

questions.prompt: At a small architecture studio, a designer's laptop keeps slowing down and then shutting off during long rendering jobs. A technician works through it. Step 1: The designer usually works with the laptop on a sofa cushion, so the technician moves it to a hard desk to keep the vents open. It still overheats. Step 2: The technician checks running programs and finds only the rendering app, which the designer must use. It still overheats. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: The laptop is five years old and still runs hot under load, so the technician replaces the dried compound between the processor and the heatsink. The shutdowns stop. Which action best fills Step 3?
choices: Recalibrate the touch input so the screen maps touches correctly
Clear built-up dust from the fan and vents, then retest under load
Replace the battery, because heat always comes from a worn battery
Replace the processor, because thermal throttling shows the chip is failing
questions.why: Dust in the fan is a cheap, common cause of overheating that should be ruled out before opening the laptop to redo the thermal paste, while throttling is a protective slowdown, not proof of a failing chip.

questions.prompt: A courier's phone is used from 100% down to 50% on Monday and then recharged to full. On Tuesday it is used from 100% down to 70% and recharged. On Wednesday it is used from 100% down to 80% and recharged. How many lithium-ion charge cycles has the battery used across these three days?
choices: Half of one, because the battery never reached 0%
One, because the partial uses add up to 100%
Three, one for each recharge
Two, because Monday's use counts as a full cycle
questions.why: A charge cycle is 100% of total use, which can be spread across partial charges, and 50% + 30% + 20% adds up to exactly one cycle.

questions.prompt: At a distribution warehouse, a worker reports that the back cover of a handheld barcode scanner has started lifting away from the body, and the battery underneath looks puffed up. What should the technician do?
choices: Take it out of service now and don't charge it or press on it
Press the cover back down firmly and tape it so dust stays out
Charge it fully, then check the battery health report for capacity
Check the power use per app to find what is draining the battery
questions.why: A swollen battery can catch fire, so it must be removed from service right away without charging it or applying pressure.

questions.prompt: A clinic's tablet registers every tap about a finger-width to the left of where the nurse actually touches. The screen is clean and dry, there is no case or screen protector, the glass is not cracked, and a restart did not help. What is the most reasonable next step?
choices: Run the touch calibration or a touch test
Replace the whole motherboard, since the input is wrong
Replace the battery, since low charge shifts touch positions
Replace the display panel, since the picture is at fault
questions.why: Touches landing in the wrong place point to calibration, the mapping between where you touch and where the device thinks you touched, which is a cheap check to run before replacing any parts.

lessons.explainPrompt: In your own words, explain to a teammate how you would troubleshoot a phone that runs hot and drains its battery quickly. Include the order of your checks and one limit or tradeoff, for example when to stop adjusting settings and replace a part.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the cheap, non-invasive checks. First I look at power use per app and the battery health report. If one app or a setting like maximum brightness is burning power, that same work is also making heat, so fixing it may solve both symptoms. Next I check the environment: is it charging while gaming, sitting in the sun, or inside a thick case that traps heat? If the device still throttles or gets hot when idle, and battery health is low, the battery is worn out from charge cycles and needs replacing. The tradeoff is that settings changes are free but can only hide a worn battery for so long. If I see any swelling, I stop immediately, don't charge it, and replace the battery because of the fire risk.
rubricPoints: Checks software and usage causes such as power use per app and brightness before replacing hardware.
Links heavy workload to both heat and battery drain.
Uses the battery health report and the idea of charge cycles to judge whether the battery is worn.
Considers environmental causes such as blocked vents, sun, cases, or charging during heavy use.
Treats a swollen battery as an immediate safety issue: no charging, no pressing, replace it.
Names a tradeoff, such as settings tweaks versus replacing the part.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine covers mobile hardware, and the core skill is reasoning from a symptom through ordered checks to a fix, which exam-style scenarios practise best.

lessons.plain: Phones and tablets run an operating system (the main software that manages the device, like iOS or Android) plus many apps. When something goes wrong, it is usually one of three things: an app keeps quitting unexpectedly (a crash), something is eating too much battery, memory or processor time (high resource use), or your mail, contacts or photos stop matching what is on the server (failed synchronization). Troubleshooting is like checking a car that will not start: you try the cheap, quick, reversible checks first, such as fuel and battery, before you take the engine apart.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user's email app crashes every time they open it, but every other app works fine. Before doing anything drastic like wiping the phone, what two or three simple things would you try first, and in what order?
lessons.teach:
Mobile OS and app troubleshooting means finding and fixing software problems on a phone or tablet by working from the least disruptive fix to the most disruptive one. That order matters because the early steps are fast and lose nothing, while the late steps erase settings or data.

For an app crash, which is an app closing unexpectedly, the usual ladder is: force stop the app (fully shut it down so it starts fresh), restart the device, clear the app's cache (temporary files the app keeps to speed things up, which can become corrupted), update the app and the OS, clear the app's data (its saved settings and local files, which is effectively a fresh install), reinstall the app, and only then consider a factory reset, which returns the whole device to its out-of-box state.

For high resource use, meaning heavy use of battery, RAM (short-term working memory) or CPU (the processor), open the battery or usage screen in settings to see which app is responsible. Then restrict its background activity, which is work it does while you are not using it, update it, or remove it. Low free storage also slows a device, so check that too.

For failed synchronization, where data no longer matches between the device and an account or server, check that there is a network connection, that the account password has not changed, that sync is switched on for that data type, that the date and time are correct (a wrong clock can break secure connections), and that storage is not full.

Worked example: a calendar stops syncing. Step one, Wi-Fi works and web pages load. Step two, the account shows a sign-in error because the user recently changed their password. Step three, re-enter the password. Sync resumes, and nothing was lost.

A common mistake is jumping straight to clearing data or a factory reset. If the user had unsynced notes or photos, those are destroyed, which turns a five-minute fix into permanent data loss.

questions.prompt: At a veterinary clinic, a receptionist's tablet has stopped syncing its email; new messages appear on the office computer but not on the tablet. A technician works through it. Step one: the tablet is on Wi-Fi and web pages load normally. Step two: the email account shows no sign-in error, and nobody has changed the password. Step three: sync is switched on for email in the account settings. Step four: the technician notices the tablet's clock reads a date two years in the past. Step five: ______. After that, email syncs again and no data was lost. What is step five?
choices: Correct the date and time, for example by setting them to update automatically
Clear the email app's data so it downloads every message again
Factory reset the tablet so the email account is set up from scratch
Restrict the email app's background activity to save battery
questions.why: A wrong clock can break secure connections, so fixing the date and time removes the cause without erasing anything.

questions.prompt: A delivery driver's phone drops from full charge to 30% by midday and feels warm, even though the driver barely touches it. Which step should come first?
choices: Open the battery or usage screen in settings to see which app is responsible
Reinstall every app that was installed in the last month
Clear the data of the phone's most-used app
Factory reset the phone to remove whatever is draining it
questions.why: For high resource use you first identify the responsible app on the battery or usage screen, then restrict, update or remove that app.

questions.prompt: A photo-editing app on a student's tablet keeps closing unexpectedly. The student has already force stopped the app and restarted the tablet, but it still crashes. Which next step is the least disruptive?
choices: Clear the app's data
Clear the app's cache
Uninstall the app and reinstall it
Perform a factory reset
questions.why: Clearing the cache only removes temporary files that may be corrupted, so it loses nothing, while clearing data, reinstalling or resetting erase saved settings or files.

questions.prompt: A note-taking app on a field engineer's phone crashes once. Without trying anything else, a technician immediately clears the app's data. The engineer had written notes that morning that had not yet synced. What is the most likely result?
choices: Nothing changes, because clearing data only affects background activity
The unsynced notes are permanently lost, because clearing data acts like a fresh install
The notes are kept, because clearing data only removes temporary files
The notes are moved to the account server automatically before the data is cleared
questions.why: Clearing data removes the app's saved settings and local files, so anything not yet synced is destroyed, which is why less disruptive steps should come first.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would troubleshoot a mobile app that keeps crashing or a device that will not sync. Include why the order of steps matters, and name one tradeoff of the more drastic fixes.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the least invasive steps and move up only if needed. For a crashing app I force stop it, restart the phone, clear its cache, then update the app and the OS. If it still crashes, I clear the app's data or reinstall it, and a factory reset is the last resort. For high battery or memory use, I check the usage screen to find the culprit app and restrict or update it. For sync failures I check connectivity, account credentials, whether sync is enabled, the date and time, and free storage. The order matters because early steps are quick and lose nothing. The tradeoff is that clearing data, reinstalling or resetting is more likely to work but can erase anything not yet synced, so I confirm the user's data is backed up first.
rubricPoints: Works from least disruptive to most disruptive fixes.
Distinguishes clearing cache, which is safe, from clearing data or resetting, which can lose data.
Uses the usage or battery screen to identify the app causing high resource use.
Lists sync checks: network, credentials, sync enabled, date and time, storage.
Names the tradeoff that drastic fixes risk losing unsynced data, so back up first.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine simulates a mobile device, so reasoning through exam-style symptom scenarios and choosing the least disruptive next step builds this skill best.

lessons.plain: Every computer on a network can run many services at once, such as a web server, email, and file sharing. A port is a numbered door on that computer, and each service listens behind its own door. Think of an office building: the street address gets a letter to the right building, and the suite number gets it to the right company inside. The IP address is the street address and the port is the suite number. Many common services use standard, agreed numbers, so learning which number belongs to which service lets you read firewall rules and spot blocked traffic quickly.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user can open a website by typing its numeric IP address but not by typing its name. Which kind of service, one that turns names into addresses, do you suspect is failing?
lessons.teach:
A port is a number from 0 to 65535 that tells the receiving computer which program should get an arriving message. The IP address picks the computer, and the port picks the service. A protocol is the agreed set of rules that a service speaks. Two transport protocols carry the data. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) sets up a connection first, confirms delivery, and resends lost pieces, so it suits web pages, email and file transfer. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) sends without confirming, which is lighter and faster, so it suits quick lookups and streaming. Well-known services listen on fixed numbers, which is how a client knows where to knock.

These are the ports to memorize. FTP (File Transfer Protocol) uses 20 and 21 TCP. SSH (Secure Shell), an encrypted remote command line, uses 22 TCP. Telnet, an unencrypted remote command line, uses 23 TCP. SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), which sends email, uses 25 TCP. DNS (Domain Name System), which turns names into IP addresses, uses 53 UDP and TCP. DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol), which hands out addresses, uses 67 and 68 UDP. HTTP, unencrypted web traffic, uses 80 TCP. POP3, which downloads mail to one device, uses 110 TCP. NetBIOS, an older Windows naming service, uses 137 to 139. IMAP, which keeps mail synced on the server, uses 143 TCP. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol), which monitors devices, uses 161 and 162 UDP. LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), used for directory lookups, uses 389. HTTPS, encrypted web traffic, uses 443 TCP. SMB (Server Message Block), Windows file and printer sharing, uses 445 TCP. RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol), full graphical remote control, uses 3389 TCP.

Here is a worked example. A user can browse by IP address but not by name. First, browsing by address works, so web traffic on 80 and 443 is fine. Second, turning names into addresses is the job of DNS. Third, you check whether port 53 is blocked or the DNS server is unreachable.

A common mistake is mixing up similar pairs, such as SSH 22 with Telnet 23, or POP3 110 with IMAP 143. If a firewall rule opens the wrong number, the real service stays unreachable while an unneeded door sits open.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm reports that staff can still read new email on their laptops, but every message they try to send sits in the outbox. A technician works through it. Step 1: Reading new mail works, so the mail-download service (POP3 on 110 TCP or IMAP on 143 TCP) is fine. Step 2: Sending email is the job of SMTP. Step 3: ______. Which choice correctly completes step 3?
choices: Check whether port 53 UDP is blocked, because DNS must resolve the mail server's name
Check whether port 110 TCP is blocked, because POP3 downloads the mail
Check whether port 25 TCP is blocked or the outgoing mail server is unreachable
Check whether port 143 TCP is blocked, because IMAP keeps mail synced on the server
questions.why: SMTP is the service that sends email and it listens on port 25 TCP, so a blocked 25 or an unreachable sending server matches a symptom where receiving works but sending fails.

questions.prompt: A packet arrives at a file server with a destination IP address and a destination port number. What job does the port number do?
choices: It decides whether the data is sent with TCP or with UDP
It tells the receiving computer which program or service should get the message
It identifies which computer on the network should receive the packet
It encrypts the message so only the right service can read it
questions.why: The IP address picks the computer, and the port number picks which service on that computer gets the message.

questions.prompt: A clinic's network administrator wants to manage a branch router from home using an encrypted text-based remote command line. Which port should the firewall allow?
choices: 3389 TCP
22 TCP
23 TCP
443 TCP
questions.why: SSH is the encrypted remote command line and uses port 22 TCP, while 23 is unencrypted Telnet and 3389 is graphical RDP.

questions.prompt: A school wants staff mail to stay synced on the server so it looks the same on phones and desktops. A technician adds a firewall rule opening port 110 TCP for this. What is the result?
choices: Synced mail works, because 110 and 143 are interchangeable mail ports
The synced-mail service (IMAP, 143 TCP) stays unreachable while an unneeded port is opened
Mail works but only over UDP, because 110 is a UDP port
Sending mail stops, because 110 replaces the SMTP port
questions.why: Port 110 is POP3, but server-synced mail is IMAP on 143 TCP, so opening the wrong number leaves the real service blocked and an unneeded door open.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a port number is, why TCP and UDP are both used, and how knowing port numbers helps you troubleshoot. Name one limit or tradeoff of relying on standard port numbers.
lessons.modelAnswer: An IP address gets traffic to the right machine, and the port number gets it to the right service on that machine. Standard services use agreed numbers. Web traffic uses 80, or 443 when it is encrypted. SSH uses 22, DNS uses 53, and RDP uses 3389. TCP confirms delivery and resends lost data, so it is used where every byte matters, like web pages, email and SMB file sharing. UDP skips the confirmation, so it is faster and lighter, which fits DNS lookups, DHCP and SNMP. When something fails, the symptom points to a service, and the service points to a port I can check in a firewall rule. If names don't resolve but IP addresses work, I look at port 53. One limit is that a standard number is only a convention. A service can be moved to another port, so the number alone does not prove what is actually running. Also, an open port is not automatically secure, because Telnet on 23 sends everything unencrypted.
rubricPoints: A port identifies the service on a host while the IP address identifies the host.
TCP is connection-based and confirms delivery, while UDP is lighter and does not confirm.
Correctly matches several common services to their ports, such as 22 SSH, 53 DNS, 443 HTTPS and 3389 RDP.
Uses a symptom-to-service-to-port chain to troubleshoot.
Names a limit, such as nonstandard ports or the fact that an open port is not the same as a secure one.

suggested.rationale: Matching port numbers to services is mainly factual recall, and no listed mission or planned engine drills it directly, so reading and self-quizzing on the list works best.

lessons.plain: A small office network is built from a few boxes, each with one job. A switch connects wired devices in the same place so they can talk to each other. A router connects that local network to other networks, such as the internet, and chooses where traffic goes next. An access point lets wireless devices join the wired network. A patch panel is an unpowered row of jacks where the building's wall cables end, so connections can be rearranged neatly. Think of an office building: the switch is the internal mail room, the router handles mail leaving the building, the access point is a drop box for visitors, and the patch panel is a labeled wall of pigeonholes.
lessons.guessPrompt: An office has ten wired desks and a printer all plugged into one box, and they can print to each other fine, but nobody can reach any website. Which kind of box do you think is missing, and why?
lessons.teach:
A LAN (local area network) is the set of devices in one home or office. Every network card has a MAC address, a fixed hardware address, and an IP address, a logical address that says which network the device belongs to. Data on a LAN travels in small chunks called frames.

A switch joins wired devices on one LAN. It watches incoming frames, records which MAC address arrived on which port in its MAC address table, then sends each frame only out of the port where the destination lives. If it does not know yet, it floods the frame to all ports once. An unmanaged switch is plug-and-play; a managed switch can be configured and monitored. The older hub simply repeated everything to every port, wasting bandwidth.

A router joins different networks. It reads the destination IP address and forwards traffic toward the right network, for example out to the internet provider. The router address a device uses to leave its LAN is its default gateway. A home router is usually a router, switch, access point and firewall in one box.

An access point (AP) bridges radio to wire: it lets Wi-Fi devices join the existing LAN, but on its own it does not route. A patch panel is passive hardware: wall cables are punched into its back, and short patch cables run from its front jacks to the switch.

Worked example: a Wi-Fi laptop prints to a wired printer. The AP receives the radio signal and puts the frame on the wire. The switch looks up the printer's MAC, sends it out one port, through the patch panel and wall jack, to the printer. Next the laptop opens a website. That IP is not local, so the laptop sends it to the default gateway, and the router forwards it to the provider.

Common mistake: plugging the internet provider's line into a plain switch. Local devices still talk, but nothing knows how to reach outside networks, so the internet is down for everyone.

questions.prompt: A small bakery office has just powered on a brand-new unmanaged switch, so its MAC address table is empty. The owner's PC is on port 3 and the shop's wired label printer is on port 7. The PC sends a frame addressed to the printer's MAC address. Trace what the switch does. Step 1: the frame arrives on port 3, so the switch records the PC's MAC address against port 3 in its MAC address table. Step 2: the switch looks up the printer's MAC address and finds no entry for it yet. Step 3: ??? Step 4: the printer replies, and the switch records the printer's MAC address against port 7. Step 5: from now on, frames for the printer go out of port 7 only. What happens in Step 3?
choices: The switch floods the frame out of all its other ports once, so the printer still receives it.
The switch hands the frame to the default gateway so the router can find the printer.
The switch sends the frame back to the patch panel, which picks the correct wall jack.
The switch drops the frame and waits until the printer announces itself first.
questions.why: When a switch does not yet know which port a destination MAC address lives on, it floods that frame to all its ports once, and it learns the correct port from the reply.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic has its staff computers on one local network and needs traffic to reach the internet provider's separate network. Which device reads the destination IP address of the traffic and forwards it toward the correct network?
choices: A router
A patch panel
A switch
An access point
questions.why: A router joins different networks by reading the destination IP address and forwarding traffic toward the right network, such as out to the internet provider.

questions.prompt: At a four-person accounting firm, someone replaced the failed all-in-one home router with a plain unmanaged switch and plugged the internet provider's line into it. Staff can still open shared folders on each other's PCs, but no one can load any website. What best explains this?
choices: The switch is unmanaged, so it cannot send frames between local PCs until it is configured.
The switch is flooding every frame to all ports, which uses up the internet bandwidth.
The patch panel needs re-punching, because it decides which cables can reach the internet.
Nothing on the network can route traffic to outside networks, because a switch does not route.
questions.why: A switch only joins devices on one LAN, so local traffic still works, but without a router no device can reach outside networks like the internet.

questions.prompt: A warehouse plugs a standalone access point (AP) into its existing wired switch so that handheld scanners can use Wi-Fi. Which statement correctly describes the access point's role?
choices: It works like a hub, repeating every frame from the wired network out to all wireless devices.
It is passive hardware, so the scanners' frames pass through it the way cables pass through a patch panel.
It bridges radio to wire, letting the scanners join the existing LAN, but on its own it does not route.
It replaces the router, so the scanners use the access point as their way out to the internet.
questions.why: An access point bridges Wi-Fi devices onto the existing wired LAN, but by itself it does not route traffic between networks.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a switch, router, access point and patch panel each do in a small office, and name one tradeoff of using a single all-in-one home router instead of separate devices.
lessons.modelAnswer: A switch connects wired devices on the same local network; it learns which hardware (MAC) address sits on which port and sends traffic only where it needs to go. A router connects our network to other networks like the internet, forwarding traffic by IP address; it is the default gateway devices use to leave the LAN. An access point puts Wi-Fi devices onto the same wired network but does not route by itself. A patch panel is just an unpowered termination point for the building's wall cables, so we can re-patch desks to switch ports neatly. An all-in-one home router is cheap and simple because it combines router, switch, AP and firewall, but it has few ports, limited Wi-Fi coverage and is a single point of failure: if it dies, wired, wireless and internet access all go down together.
rubricPoints: A switch connects devices within one LAN and forwards by MAC address to the correct port.
A router connects different networks and forwards by IP address, acting as the default gateway.
An access point bridges wireless clients onto the wired LAN and does not route by itself.
A patch panel is passive and only terminates and organizes cable runs.
Names a real tradeoff, such as the all-in-one router being a single point of failure or having limited ports and coverage.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by describing an office situation and asking which device fits or is missing, so reasoning through short scenarios builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Wi-Fi is a family of rules, called 802.11 standards, that let devices talk by radio instead of by cable. Each new generation got faster and smarter, and they use different radio bands: 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz and, most recently, 6 GHz. Think of the bands like roads. 2.4 GHz is a long country road that reaches far and passes through walls but gets crowded. 5 and 6 GHz are wide highways that are faster but do not reach as far. Encryption, such as WPA2 or WPA3, scrambles the radio traffic so neighbours cannot read it or join your network without the password.
lessons.guessPrompt: A home router offers two networks, one on 2.4 GHz and one on 5 GHz. A laptop two rooms and three walls away keeps dropping off the 5 GHz network. Which band would you try, and why?
lessons.teach:
An 802.11 standard is a published rulebook for wireless networking. The marketing names (Wi-Fi 4, 5, 6, 7) map onto them. 802.11a used 5 GHz at up to 54 Mbps. 802.11b used 2.4 GHz at 11 Mbps, and 802.11g kept 2.4 GHz but reached 54 Mbps. 802.11n (Wi-Fi 4) works on both 2.4 and 5 GHz and added MIMO, meaning several antennas sending at once. 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5) is 5 GHz only and reaches gigabit-class speeds. 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) uses 2.4 and 5 GHz and handles crowded rooms better; Wi-Fi 6E extends it to 6 GHz. 802.11be (Wi-Fi 7) uses all three bands.

Why bands differ: lower frequencies travel farther and pass through walls more easily. 2.4 GHz has long range but only three non-overlapping channels (1, 6, 11) and shares the air with microwaves and Bluetooth. 5 GHz has many more channels and higher speed but shorter range. 6 GHz is the cleanest but shortest-range.

Encryption: WEP and the original WPA with TKIP are broken and should never be chosen. WPA2 uses AES, a strong cipher. WPA3 replaces the WPA2 password exchange with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), which resists offline password guessing, and is required on 6 GHz. Both come in Personal mode (a shared passphrase) and Enterprise mode (each user logs in through an authentication server, usually RADIUS, using 802.1X).

Worked example: a small office has new Wi-Fi 6 laptops and an old 802.11g printer. Step 1: the printer only speaks 2.4 GHz, so 2.4 GHz must stay on. Step 2: put laptops on 5 GHz for speed. Step 3: set 2.4 GHz to channel 1, 6 or 11 after checking neighbours. Step 4: choose WPA3, or WPA2/WPA3 transition mode if the printer cannot do WPA3, never TKIP.

Common mistake: assuming 5 GHz is always better. Far from the router, a slower 2.4 GHz link that stays connected beats a fast one that keeps dropping, and users experience the drops as an outage.

questions.prompt: A public library adds a Wi-Fi 6E access point so its new staff laptops can use the 6 GHz band. Step 1: confirm that every staff laptop supports Wi-Fi 6E, because only 6E-capable devices can use 6 GHz. Step 2: mount the access point inside the staff workroom, because 6 GHz has the shortest range of the three bands. Step 3: (missing) choose the security setting for the 6 GHz network. Step 4: keep a separate 5 GHz network running for the library's older Wi-Fi 5 tablets, because Wi-Fi 5 cannot use 6 GHz. What is the correct Step 3?
choices: Use WPA2/WPA3 transition mode on 6 GHz so older devices can also join it
Use WPA2 with AES, because AES is a strong cipher and works on every band
Use the original WPA with TKIP, because the oldest option gives the widest compatibility
Use WPA3, because WPA3 is required on 6 GHz and its SAE exchange resists offline password guessing
questions.why: WPA3 is required on the 6 GHz band, so WPA2 alone or a WPA2/WPA3 transition mode is not allowed there, and TKIP is broken and should never be chosen.

questions.prompt: A shop owner has a laptop that connects using 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5). The router is currently set to broadcast only on 2.4 GHz. Which band must the owner turn on so the laptop can make an 802.11ac connection?
choices: 2.4 GHz, because 802.11ac uses the same band as 802.11g
Any band, because 802.11ac uses all three bands
6 GHz, because 802.11ac was the first standard to add 6 GHz
5 GHz, because 802.11ac works only on 5 GHz
questions.why: 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5) is a 5 GHz-only standard, so the router must offer 5 GHz for an 802.11ac link.

questions.prompt: In a warehouse, a staff member's handheld scanner sits at the far end of the building, a long way from the router and behind several walls. It is joined to the 5 GHz network and keeps disconnecting every few minutes. The staff member reports that the Wi-Fi is down. What is the best change to make?
choices: Leave it on 5 GHz, because 5 GHz has more channels and is always the better choice
Switch the network's security from WPA2 to WEP to make connecting easier
Connect the scanner to 2.4 GHz, because lower frequencies reach farther and pass through walls more easily
Move the scanner to 6 GHz, because 6 GHz is the cleanest band
questions.why: At long range through walls, a slower 2.4 GHz link that stays connected works better than a faster 5 GHz link that keeps dropping, and users experience those drops as an outage.

questions.prompt: An accounting firm with 40 employees wants every person to sign in to Wi-Fi with their own credentials. When someone leaves the firm, IT wants to cut off only that person without changing a password everyone shares. Which setup fits this need?
choices: WPA3-Enterprise, where each user logs in through an authentication server such as RADIUS using 802.1X
WPA2-Personal with AES and a passphrase printed on each desk
WPA3-Personal with one strong shared passphrase that is changed every month
WEP with a separate key for each department
questions.why: Enterprise mode authenticates each user individually through a server such as RADIUS using 802.1X, so one account can be disabled without affecting anyone else, while Personal mode relies on a single shared passphrase.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would pick a band and a security setting for a small office Wi-Fi network, including one tradeoff you would accept and why.
lessons.modelAnswer: Wi-Fi generations are 802.11 standards, newer ones being faster: n is Wi-Fi 4 on 2.4 and 5 GHz, ac is Wi-Fi 5 on 5 GHz only, ax is Wi-Fi 6, with 6E adding 6 GHz. The band choice is a range-versus-speed tradeoff. 2.4 GHz reaches far and through walls but is crowded and has only three clean channels, 1, 6 and 11. 5 GHz and 6 GHz are faster with more channels but cover less distance. So I would put modern laptops near the router on 5 GHz and keep 2.4 GHz for distant spots or old devices. For security I would pick WPA3, which uses SAE to resist password guessing, or WPA2 with AES if an older device needs it, accepting slightly weaker protection for compatibility. I would never use WEP or TKIP. Enterprise mode with RADIUS is better than a shared passphrase if staff come and go.
rubricPoints: Maps at least some 802.11 letters to bands or Wi-Fi generation names.
States that 2.4 GHz trades speed for range and wall penetration while 5/6 GHz trade range for speed and channels.
Mentions the non-overlapping 2.4 GHz channels 1, 6 and 11.
Prefers WPA3 (SAE) or WPA2 with AES and rejects WEP and TKIP.
Distinguishes Personal (shared passphrase) from Enterprise (802.1X with RADIUS).
Names a concrete tradeoff such as compatibility with older devices versus stronger security.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine configures Wi-Fi, so reasoning through exam-style office scenarios that pair devices with bands and security modes builds the judgment the exam tests.

lessons.plain: Every device on a network needs an address, like a house number, so traffic can find it. A small office or home router can hand these out automatically or you can set them by hand. Because your internet provider usually gives you only one public address, the router also acts like a receptionist: everyone inside shares that one outside number, and the receptionist remembers who asked for what so replies reach the right desk. The router's firewall decides which visitors get in at all, and port forwarding is a standing instruction telling the receptionist to send one kind of outside visitor straight to one particular desk.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your home has one public internet address, yet a dozen phones, laptops and TVs are online at the same time. How do you think a reply from a website finds its way back to the one device that asked for it?
lessons.teach:
A SOHO (small office/home office) router hands out and translates addresses for every device behind it. An IP address is a device's numeric network address. With DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol), the router automatically leases each device an address, a subnet mask, a default gateway (the router's own inside address) and a DNS server. Leases expire and a device may get a different address later. A static address is typed in by hand and never changes, which suits printers, servers and the router itself. A DHCP reservation is a middle path: the router always gives the same address to one device, recognised by its MAC address (the hardware ID of its network card). Static addresses must sit outside the DHCP pool (the range the router hands out), or two devices may clash.

Inside devices use private addresses such as 192.168.1.x, which cannot travel across the internet. NAT (Network Address Translation) lets them share the single public address the provider gives the router. Outgoing traffic is rewritten to show the public address, and the router records each conversation so replies return to the right device. A side effect is that unrequested inbound traffic matches no conversation and is dropped.

A firewall rule allows or blocks traffic based on address, protocol and port number (a number identifying a service on a device). Port forwarding is a rule that sends inbound traffic on a chosen public port to a specific inside address and port.

Worked example: an office wants to reach a camera recorder at 192.168.1.50 on TCP port 8443 from outside. First, give the recorder a reservation or a static address outside the pool. Second, create a forward from public TCP 8443 to 192.168.1.50 port 8443. Third, confirm the firewall permits it. A request reaching the public address on 8443 is now translated and delivered.

Common mistake: forwarding to an address DHCP assigned dynamically. After a reboot the recorder becomes 192.168.1.73, the forward points at nothing, and remote access silently breaks. Every forward also exposes that device to the internet, so open only what is truly needed.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm's router has the public address 203.0.113.9. Inside, a laptop at 192.168.5.12 requests a web page from an internet server. Trace what NAT does. Step 1: The laptop sends the request to its default gateway, the router's inside address. Step 2: The router rewrites the request's source address from 192.168.5.12 to the public address 203.0.113.9. Step 3: The router records the conversation, noting that this exchange belongs to 192.168.5.12. Step 4: The web server's reply arrives at 203.0.113.9. Step 5: ??? Step 6: The laptop displays the page. Which choice correctly fills in Step 5?
choices: The router drops the reply, because NAT discards all inbound traffic arriving at the public address.
The router sends a copy of the reply to every inside device, and the laptop keeps the copy meant for it.
The router matches the reply to its recorded conversation and delivers it to 192.168.5.12.
The router passes the reply to the DNS server, which works out which inside device should receive it.
