questions.why: NAT records each outgoing conversation so that a reply to the public address can be matched and sent back to the inside device that started it. Only unrequested inbound traffic, which matches no record, is dropped.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic wants its label printer to always have the same IP address. The manager wants to set this up centrally on the router rather than typing settings into the printer itself. Which approach fits best?
choices: Create a DHCP reservation on the router that ties one address to the printer's MAC address.
Enable NAT so the printer shares the router's public address.
Create a port forward from a public port to the printer's current address.
Shorten the DHCP lease time so the printer renews its address more often.
questions.why: A DHCP reservation makes the router always lease the same address to one device, which it recognises by its MAC address (the hardware ID of its network card). The router still hands out the address, so the setup stays central.

questions.prompt: At a design studio, the router's DHCP pool is 192.168.8.100 to 192.168.8.199. A technician gives a new storage server the static address 192.168.8.120. A few days later, the server and a staff laptop start having intermittent connection problems. What is the best fix?
choices: Turn off NAT so the two devices stop sharing the public address.
Add a firewall rule that blocks the laptop's port numbers.
Give the server a static address outside the pool, such as 192.168.8.20.
Change the default gateway on the server to 192.168.8.120.
questions.why: The static address sat inside the DHCP pool, so the router could also lease 192.168.8.120 to another device and cause a clash. A static address placed outside the pool avoids this.

questions.prompt: A hobbyist runs a game server on a home PC at 192.168.1.40. Friends on the internet type in the router's public address, but they cannot connect. No port forwarding rule has been created. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The PC's DHCP lease has expired, so the PC no longer has any IP address.
The router's DNS server setting is blocking all incoming game traffic.
Their connection attempts are unrequested inbound traffic that matches no NAT conversation, so the router drops them.
Private addresses like 192.168.1.40 are not allowed to run server software.
questions.why: NAT only knows where to deliver inbound traffic that answers a conversation an inside device started. With no port forward, the friends' connection attempts match nothing, so the router drops them.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why the office printer and the camera recorder need fixed addresses when everything else uses DHCP, and why remote access to the recorder needs a port forward. Explain it in your own words, including one risk or tradeoff of port forwarding.
lessons.modelAnswer: Most devices are fine with DHCP: the router leases them an address, gateway and DNS automatically, and if the address changes nobody cares. The printer and recorder are different because other things point at them by address. If DHCP gives them a new address, those pointers break. So we either set a static address outside the DHCP pool or create a DHCP reservation tied to their MAC address. Remote access needs a forward because of NAT: all inside devices share one public address, and the router only lets in replies to conversations started from inside. An outside request to the recorder matches nothing and gets dropped, so we add a rule sending public TCP 8443 to the recorder's inside address and port, and allow it in the firewall. The tradeoff is exposure: anyone on the internet can now reach that device, so we forward only what is needed and keep it patched.
rubricPoints: DHCP assigns addresses automatically and they can change, while static or reserved addresses stay fixed.
Static addresses should be outside the DHCP pool, or a reservation should be tied to the device's MAC address.
NAT lets private inside addresses share one public address and drops unrequested inbound traffic.
Port forwarding maps a public port to a specific inside address and port, and the firewall must allow it.
Forwarding to a changing DHCP address breaks access after the address changes.
Each forward exposes a device to the internet, so open only what is needed.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine configures a SOHO router, and the exam tests this by asking you to reason through office scenarios about addressing, NAT and forwards, so worked scenarios add the most.

lessons.plain: A small office router can do more than just share an internet connection. A VPN builds a private, scrambled tunnel across the internet so a worker at home can use the office network safely. A VLAN splits one physical network into separate virtual ones, so guests and staff share the same equipment without seeing each other's devices. QoS, short for quality of service, decides which traffic goes first when the connection is busy. Think of a busy road: the VPN is a covered private lane, VLANs are separate fenced lots in one car park, and QoS is the rule that lets the ambulance pass first.
lessons.guessPrompt: An office has one internet connection. Someone starts a huge file download, and everyone's video calls begin to stutter. Without buying a faster connection, what kind of router setting do you think could keep the calls smooth, and what would it have to do?
lessons.teach:
A SOHO (small office/home office) router usually offers three features that control where traffic goes and how it is treated. A VPN (virtual private network) creates an encrypted tunnel across the internet so a remote device behaves as if it were plugged into the office. Encrypted means the data is scrambled so only the two ends of the tunnel can read it. A VLAN (virtual local area network) divides one physical router or switch into separate logical networks. Each VLAN has its own broadcast area and usually its own subnet, which is a range of addresses. Devices on different VLANs cannot talk to each other unless the router allows it. QoS (quality of service) ranks traffic by device, application or port, so the router sends important traffic first when the internet link is full.

These features work for different reasons. The VPN tunnel hides traffic from anyone in between. A VLAN tag, a small label added to each frame under the 802.1Q standard, lets one cable carry several separate networks. QoS reorders the queue of waiting traffic, but it does not create extra bandwidth.

Here is a worked example. A dental office reports two problems: video calls stutter, and guests on Wi-Fi can see the office printer. Step 1: check the VLANs. Guests and staff are on the same VLAN, so create a guest VLAN and map the guest wireless network name to it. Step 2: confirm that a guest phone now gets an address from the guest subnet and can no longer reach the printer. Step 3: in the QoS settings, give the video-calling application or the staff laptops high priority. Step 4: test by running a large download during a call. The call should stay smooth. Step 5: the owner's VPN from home also fails. Check that the VPN is enabled, that the username and pre-shared key (a shared password) match on both ends, and that the router firewall allows the VPN ports.

A common mistake is using QoS to fix a link that is simply too slow. QoS only helps when the link is congested. If every kind of traffic is marked high priority, nothing is actually prioritized. In a running office, a device put on the wrong VLAN either gets cut off without warning or ends up exposing sensitive equipment to guests.

questions.prompt: A four-person architecture studio says its video meetings freeze whenever someone uploads large drawing files to a client. The technician works through it. Step 1: watch the router's traffic graph during an upload. The internet link sits at full capacity, so the link is congested. Step 2: since the link is congested, QoS is a reasonable fix, because it can reorder the waiting traffic. Step 3: in the QoS settings, give the video-meeting application high priority and leave file uploads at normal priority. Step 4: ? Which choice best completes Step 4?
choices: Turn on QoS bandwidth expansion so that the link can carry the uploads and the meeting together.
Start a large upload during a test meeting and confirm that the meeting stays smooth.
Move the upload computer to a guest VLAN so that its traffic no longer uses the internet link.
Mark the file uploads high priority as well, so that both kinds of traffic are treated as important.
questions.why: After changing QoS you check the fix under real load, and a smooth meeting during a heavy upload shows the priority setting works.

questions.prompt: A small warehouse runs one cable between its router and a switch. That cable must carry both the staff network and a separate scanner network. What lets one cable keep the two networks apart?
choices: An 802.1Q VLAN tag, which is a small label added to each frame that marks which network the frame belongs to.
A pre-shared key that encrypts each network's traffic so that the other network cannot read it.
A QoS rule that sends the staff traffic first and holds the scanner traffic until the link is idle.
A VPN tunnel that runs between the router and the switch for each network.
questions.why: VLAN tags under 802.1Q label each frame with its VLAN, so one cable can carry several separate logical networks.

questions.prompt: A home-based bookkeeper has a very slow internet plan. Downloads crawl even when only one laptop is online and nothing else is running. She asks whether turning on QoS will make her connection faster. What is the best answer?
choices: Yes, but only if every application is marked high priority.
Yes. QoS adds extra bandwidth for any device that is marked high priority.
No. QoS only reorders traffic when the link is congested, and it cannot make a link that is simply too slow any faster.
Yes. A VPN combined with QoS compresses the traffic so that it moves faster.
questions.why: QoS only ranks traffic waiting in a full queue. It creates no extra bandwidth, so it cannot fix a link that is too slow even when idle.

questions.prompt: At a small café, a technician sets up two VLANs: one for the payment terminals and one for customer Wi-Fi. The technician accidentally assigns a payment terminal to the customer VLAN. What is the most likely result?
choices: The terminal keeps working normally, because VLANs only change how traffic is prioritized.
Nothing changes, because devices on different VLANs can always talk to each other.
The terminal's traffic becomes encrypted, because guest VLANs automatically create a VPN.
The terminal is cut off from the payment network or exposed to customers, because it now sits in the customers' separate network and subnet.
questions.why: Each VLAN is its own separate network, so a device on the wrong VLAN can lose access without warning or expose sensitive equipment to guests.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what VPN, VLAN and QoS each do on a small office router, and name one limit or tradeoff of at least one of them.
lessons.modelAnswer: These three settings solve different problems. A VPN builds an encrypted tunnel over the internet, so someone working from home can reach office resources as if they were on site. The tradeoff is that both ends must agree on settings like the shared key, and the firewall has to let the VPN through, or the tunnel never comes up. A VLAN splits one physical network into separate logical networks with their own address ranges. That is how we keep guest Wi-Fi away from the printer and the file server. Put a device on the wrong VLAN, though, and it quietly loses access. QoS ranks traffic so calls or key devices go first when the link is busy. Its main limit is that it only reorders traffic and never adds bandwidth. If the line is simply too slow, or everything is marked high priority, QoS won't help.
rubricPoints: States that a VPN is an encrypted tunnel letting a remote device act as if it were on the office network.
States that a VLAN separates one physical network into isolated logical networks, each usually with its own subnet.
States that QoS prioritizes certain traffic when the link is congested.
Names a limit, such as QoS adding no bandwidth, VPN settings needing to match on both ends, or a wrong VLAN cutting a device off.
Connects at least one setting to a realistic office symptom like stuttering calls or guests reaching private devices.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine configures a SOHO router, so reasoning through exam-style office scenarios that need the right VPN, VLAN or QoS fix builds this skill best.

lessons.plain: An internet connection type is the physical path that carries your home or office traffic to your internet service provider (ISP), the company that sells you internet access. The five common kinds are cable (TV coaxial wire), DSL (telephone wire), fiber (glass strands carrying light), satellite (a dish talking to a spacecraft) and cellular (a mobile phone network). Think of them as different roads into town: some are wide motorways, some are narrow country lanes, and some are long bridges where every trip takes time even when traffic is light. Choosing well means matching the road to where you live and what you need to do.
lessons.guessPrompt: A remote cabin has no phone or TV cables nearby, and the owner wants to make smooth video calls. Which connection would you try first, cellular or a traditional satellite dish, and why might the satellite feel sluggish even if its download speed looks good?
lessons.teach:
Two measurements separate these connections. Bandwidth is how much data per second the link can carry. Latency is the delay for one piece of data to make a round trip, measured in milliseconds. Many links are asymmetric, meaning download bandwidth is much higher than upload; symmetric means both directions are equal.

Cable uses the coaxial copper wire built for cable TV, with a cable modem converting the signal. It is fast and widely available, but neighbours share the same local line, so speeds can drop at busy evening hours. It is usually asymmetric.

DSL (digital subscriber line) sends data over ordinary telephone wire. It is cheap and common in older areas, but speed falls as distance from the provider's local exchange grows, and it is slower than cable or fiber. ADSL is the asymmetric form.

Fiber carries pulses of light through glass strands. It offers the highest bandwidth, low latency, often symmetric speeds and immunity to electrical interference, but it costs the most to build, so availability is limited.

Satellite needs only a dish with a clear view of the sky, so it reaches remote places. Traditional satellites sit very far away in a fixed (geostationary) orbit, giving high latency, often over 500 ms round trip. Newer low-orbit constellations cut that delay a lot. Heavy rain or snow can disrupt the signal.

Cellular uses mobile networks (4G, 5G) through a phone hotspot or a cellular router. It is quick to set up and portable, but speed depends on signal strength, and plans often have data caps.

Worked example: a small office needs to send large video files to clients daily. Step one: the main traffic is upload. Step two: cable and DSL are typically asymmetric, so uploads are slow. Step three: fiber is often symmetric and available at their address. Choice: fiber.

Common mistake: treating bandwidth as the only measure. A high-latency satellite link can download quickly yet make voice calls, video meetings and remote desktop sessions lag badly, so users complain that the network is broken when the link is simply slow to respond.

questions.prompt: A rural veterinary clinic has no cable, DSL or fiber service at its address. The vets run live video consultations with pet owners all day, so delays in the conversation matter more than raw download speed. Step one: the key need is low latency (a short round-trip delay) for live video. Step two: wired options are unavailable, but satellite needs only a dish with a clear view of the sky, so it can reach the clinic. Step three: ______. Choice: a low-orbit satellite service. Which statement correctly fills step three?
choices: Satellite bandwidth is always higher than cellular bandwidth, so any satellite service will make the video calls smooth.
Satellite is immune to weather, so the only thing to compare between services is the monthly price.
Traditional geostationary satellites are very far away and often exceed 500 ms round trip, while low-orbit constellations cut that delay a lot.
Geostationary and low-orbit satellites sit at the same distance, so latency will be about the same whichever service they pick.
questions.why: For live video, latency is the deciding factor, and low-orbit satellites have far less round-trip delay than distant geostationary ones.

questions.prompt: A technician says a connection has 40 ms of latency. What is that number describing?
choices: How far the building is from the provider's local exchange
How much data per second the link can carry in the download direction
The delay for one piece of data to make a round trip across the link
The difference between the link's upload and download speeds
questions.why: Latency is the round-trip delay for data, measured in milliseconds. Bandwidth is the amount of data per second.

questions.prompt: A construction company sets up a temporary site office in a trailer for six weeks. There is no wired service, and the trailer will move to another site afterwards. Staff mainly send emails and check plans. Which connection type fits best?
choices: Fiber, because it has the highest bandwidth and lowest latency
Cable, because it is fast and widely available
DSL, because it is cheap and runs over ordinary telephone wire
Cellular through a cellular router, because it is quick to set up and portable
questions.why: Cellular needs no installed wiring and moves with the trailer. The main thing to watch is the plan's data cap.

questions.prompt: A home user on a cable connection complains that speeds are fine in the morning but drop sharply every weekday from about 7 to 10 pm. Nothing in the house has changed. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The house is too far from the provider's local exchange, which slows the signal at night.
Rain and snow in the evening disrupt the dish's view of the sky.
The connection is symmetric, so upload traffic is crowding out downloads at night.
Neighbours share the same local cable line, so heavy evening use by many households lowers each user's speed.
questions.why: Cable is a shared local line, so busy evening hours reduce speeds. Distance from the exchange affects DSL, and weather affects satellite.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between cable, DSL, fiber, satellite and cellular for a customer, and name one tradeoff each of satellite and cable brings.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with what is available at the address, then what the customer does online. Fiber uses light over glass and is the best when available: highest bandwidth, low latency, often equal upload and download speeds. Cable runs over the TV coax line and is fast, but neighbours share the local line, so it can slow down at peak times, and upload is usually much slower than download. DSL uses phone wire; it is cheap but slower and gets worse the farther you are from the provider's exchange. Cellular is quick to set up and portable, but depends on signal and often has data caps. Satellite reaches remote places with no wires, but traditional satellites add high latency, so video calls and remote desktop feel laggy even with decent bandwidth, and bad weather can drop it.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes bandwidth from latency.
Describes the medium each type uses: coax, phone wire, glass fiber, satellite dish, mobile network.
Notes that satellite has high latency and weather sensitivity but reaches remote areas.
Notes that cable bandwidth is shared and usually asymmetric.
Identifies fiber as highest performance but limited availability, and DSL as distance-limited.
Ties the choice to the customer's location and usage, such as upload needs or real-time calls.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this through short customer scenarios, so reasoning through situations that weigh availability, latency and upload needs builds the skill better than memorising a list.

lessons.plain: When a network connection fails, the problem is often physical: a badly made cable, a loose wire in a wall jack, or a crowded wireless channel. Four hand tools let a technician check and fix these instead of guessing. A cable tester checks whether every wire in a cable connects end to end. A crimper attaches a plug to the end of a cable. A punchdown tool presses wires into a wall jack or patch panel. A Wi-Fi analyzer shows nearby wireless networks, how strong each signal is, and which channels they use. Think of it like a plumber's kit: a different tool for checking, joining and fixing the pipes.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user's desk computer suddenly shows 'network cable unplugged,' even though the cable is firmly plugged in at both ends. Before touching any settings, what would you want to check about the cable itself, and how might you check it?
lessons.teach:
These four tools troubleshoot and repair the physical layer, which means the actual cables, connectors and radio signals that carry data.

A cable tester is a two-part device. You plug one part into each end of a copper network cable and it checks each of the eight wires. It reports the wire map, meaning which pin at one end connects to which pin at the other. It flags opens (a broken wire), shorts (two wires touching) and miswires (wires in the wrong order). A crimper is a pliers-like tool that squeezes an RJ45 connector, the standard eight-pin network plug, onto the end of a cable so its metal pins bite into the wires. A punchdown tool pushes a single wire into a slot on a keystone jack (a wall or desk socket) or a patch panel (a row of jacks in a network closet), trims the excess and locks the wire in place. A Wi-Fi analyzer is software, often on a laptop or phone, that lists nearby wireless networks by SSID (the network name), their signal strength in dBm (closer to zero is stronger, so -50 beats -80) and their channels.

Worked example: a user's PC shows no link. First, swap in a known-good cable. The link comes up, so the old cable is suspect. Next, put the old cable on the tester. The wire map shows pin 3 open. Then cut off the faulty plug, put the wires in the correct order, and crimp on a new RJ45. Finally, retest. All eight pins pass, so the cable goes back into service.

A common mistake is crimping before the wires are fully pushed to the end of the plug in the right order. The cable may look fine but test as open or miswired. Also, a punched-down wire that is not seated properly can cause a link that keeps dropping, which is far harder to diagnose than a dead one. Wireless complaints work the same way. Slow Wi-Fi in a crowded building often means neighbors share your channel, and an analyzer shows you a less crowded one to move to.

questions.prompt: At a small veterinary clinic, the reception PC keeps losing its network connection for a few seconds at a time, several times an hour. The technician works through it like this. Step 1: Replace the short patch cable between the PC and the wall jack with a known-good one. The drops continue, so the patch cable is not the cause. Step 2: Connect the cable tester to the wall jack at one end and to the matching port on the patch panel in the network closet at the other end. The wire map shows pin 6 as open. When the technician looks at the back of that patch panel port, the pin 6 wire is sitting loosely in its slot. Step 3: ??? Step 4: Run the cable tester on the same run again. All eight pins pass, and the PC stops dropping. What is Step 3?
choices: Run a Wi-Fi analyzer at reception to find a less crowded channel for the PC
Swap in a second known-good patch cable at the PC to confirm that the first replacement was not faulty
Crimp a new RJ45 connector onto the back of the patch panel port so the loose wire is clamped in place
Use the punchdown tool to push the pin 6 wire fully into its patch panel slot, trimming the excess and locking it in
questions.why: A wire that is not seated properly in a patch panel slot is fixed with a punchdown tool, which pushes the wire into the slot, trims the excess and locks it in place.

questions.prompt: A technician uses a Wi-Fi analyzer in a warehouse office and sees four networks with these signal strengths: Stockroom at -72 dBm, Office-Main at -45 dBm, Loading at -88 dBm and Guest at -60 dBm. Which network has the strongest signal at the technician's location?
choices: Stockroom, because -72 dBm is in the middle of the range
Guest, because -60 dBm is the average of the readings
Loading, because -88 is the largest number on the list
Office-Main, because -45 dBm is the reading closest to zero
questions.why: Signal strength is measured in dBm, and a reading closer to zero means a stronger signal, so -45 dBm is the strongest of the four.

questions.prompt: Staff in a busy shared office building say the company Wi-Fi has been slow for weeks. A Wi-Fi analyzer shows the company network on channel 6, along with seven neighboring networks on the same channel. Channels 1 and 11 each have only one other network. What is the most sensible next step?
choices: Recrimp the RJ45 plug on the cable that runs to the wireless router
Move the company network to a less crowded channel, such as 1 or 11
Re-punch every wire on the patch panel to remove any loose connections
Test every desk cable with a cable tester, because slow Wi-Fi is usually caused by broken wiring
questions.why: Slow Wi-Fi in a crowded building often happens because neighbors share your channel, and the analyzer shows that channels 1 and 11 are much less crowded.

questions.prompt: A new hire at a print shop crimps an RJ45 connector onto a cable. The plug looks fine from the outside, but the cable tester's wire map reports a miswire on two of the pins. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Before crimping, the wires were not all pushed to the end of the plug in the correct order
The punchdown tool was not used to trim the extra wire at the plug
The cable tester needs a Wi-Fi analyzer to read the wire map correctly
Nearby wireless networks on the same channel are interfering with the copper wires
questions.why: Crimping before the wires are in the right order and fully seated in the plug is a common mistake, and it produces a cable that looks fine but tests as open or miswired.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide which of these four tools to grab for a connectivity complaint, and name one limit of a basic cable tester.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by matching the tool to the symptom. If a wired device has no link or keeps dropping, I suspect the cable or its termination. I put it on a cable tester, which checks all eight wires for opens, shorts or miswires. If the plug end is bad, I cut it off and fit a new RJ45 with a crimper. If the fault is at the wall jack or patch panel, I re-seat the wire with a punchdown tool. Every time I repair something, I retest. If the complaint is slow or dropping Wi-Fi, there is no cable to test. I use a Wi-Fi analyzer to check signal strength in dBm and whether neighboring networks share my channel, then move to a clearer channel. One limit: a basic tester only confirms that each wire connects. It does not prove the cable can carry full speed over its length, so a passing cable can still perform poorly.
rubricPoints: A cable tester checks the wire map for opens, shorts and miswires on copper cable.
A crimper attaches an RJ45 plug to a cable end.
A punchdown tool seats wires into keystone jacks or patch panels.
A Wi-Fi analyzer shows SSIDs, signal strength and channel use, which helps with wireless complaints.
Retest after every repair.
A basic tester has a limit, such as confirming continuity but not full-speed performance.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine handles physical cabling tools, so the skill is best built by reasoning through exam-style symptom scenarios and choosing the right tool for each.

lessons.plain: When a computer cannot reach something on the network, a few built-in text commands let you check, layer by layer, where the trouble starts instead of guessing. ipconfig (Windows) or ifconfig (Linux and macOS) shows what address the computer has. ping asks another device whether it is reachable. tracert lists every stop along the route to a destination. nslookup asks a name-lookup server what number belongs to a website name. Think of mailing a letter: check your own return address, check that the local post office answers, follow the route, and confirm the street address is right.
lessons.guessPrompt: A coworker can open a website when they type its numeric address but not when they type its name, like example.com. Which part of the network do you think is failing, and why?
lessons.teach:
These four commands each answer one question. ipconfig on Windows, and ifconfig on Linux or macOS, show the computer's IP address (its numeric network address), subnet mask (which addresses count as local), default gateway (the router that forwards traffic off the local network) and, with ipconfig /all, the DNS servers. DNS, the Domain Name System, turns names into IP addresses. An address starting 169.254 is an APIPA address: Windows assigns it to itself when DHCP, the service that hands out addresses automatically, did not answer. ipconfig /release and ipconfig /renew ask DHCP for a fresh address.

ping sends small ICMP echo messages. ICMP is a control protocol devices use for status messages. A reply with a time in milliseconds means the target is reachable. Request timed out means no answer came back. Destination host unreachable usually means a router or your own machine could not find a path. tracert, called traceroute on Linux and macOS, lists each hop, meaning each router the traffic passes through, with response times. A row of asterisks means that hop did not reply.

nslookup queries a DNS server directly and returns the IP address for a name, or an error if the lookup fails.

Here is a worked example. A user cannot browse. First, ipconfig shows 192.168.1.50 with gateway 192.168.1.1, so addressing is fine. Second, ping 192.168.1.1 replies, so the local network works. Third, ping 8.8.8.8, a public address, replies, so internet routing works. Fourth, ping example.com fails, and nslookup example.com reports that the server could not find the name. The fault is DNS, not the cable or the router.

A common mistake is deciding a host is down because ping fails. Many firewalls block ICMP, so a silent ping or asterisks in tracert can be normal. Confirm with another test before you replace hardware or blame the remote site. Working in order from your own address outward keeps a misdiagnosis from causing needless downtime.

questions.prompt: A bakery's front-counter PC cannot reach the order website or the shared printer. A technician works through it. Step 1: ipconfig shows IP address 169.254.33.7 and no default gateway. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: the technician runs ipconfig /release and then ipconfig /renew, and ipconfig now shows 10.0.0.42 with gateway 10.0.0.1. Step 4: ping 10.0.0.1 returns replies with times in milliseconds, so the local network now works. Which conclusion belongs in Step 2?
choices: DNS is failing, so the PC cannot turn the website's name into an IP address
The internet provider is down, so the router has no path off the local network
The address is APIPA, meaning DHCP did not answer and Windows assigned itself an address
The router's firewall is blocking ICMP, so the PC only appears to be disconnected
questions.why: An address starting 169.254 is one Windows gives itself when DHCP does not respond, which is why asking DHCP for a fresh address with release and renew is the logical next step.

questions.prompt: At a small law office, a technician runs ping against a supplier's web server and gets Request timed out four times. However, the supplier's website loads normally in the browser on the same computer. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The supplier's web server is down and the browser is showing an old saved copy of the page
The office's DNS server is returning the wrong IP address for the supplier's website
The office PC has an APIPA address and cannot reach anything outside the office
The supplier's firewall blocks ICMP echo messages, so ping gets no answer even though the server is up
questions.why: Many firewalls block ICMP, so a silent ping can be normal; the working website is a second test that confirms the server is reachable.

questions.prompt: A technician at a veterinary clinic needs to see which DNS servers a Windows workstation is set to use, along with its IP address and default gateway. Which command shows all of this?
choices: ping with the DNS server's name
tracert to the default gateway
ipconfig /all
nslookup with no other test
questions.why: Plain ipconfig shows the address, subnet mask and gateway, and adding /all also lists the DNS servers the computer uses.

questions.prompt: A technician at a print shop runs tracert to a cloud backup service. Hops 1 to 3 show response times, hop 4 shows only asterisks, and hops 5 to 9 show response times, with the last hop being the backup service. What does hop 4 tell the technician?
choices: The router at hop 4 did not reply to the trace, but traffic still passed through it
DNS failed at hop 4, so the backup service's name could not be turned into an address
The path is broken at hop 4, so the traffic never reaches the backup service
The print shop's own computer has lost its default gateway partway through the trace
questions.why: A row of asterisks only means that hop did not reply, and because later hops answered, traffic clearly continued past it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use ipconfig, ping, tracert and nslookup, in order, to find where a 'no internet' problem starts, and name one limit of these tools.
lessons.modelAnswer: I work from my own machine outward. First, ipconfig, or ifconfig on Linux, shows whether I have a valid IP address, subnet mask, gateway and DNS server. If the address starts with 169.254, DHCP failed, so I try ipconfig /release and /renew and check the link. Next, I ping the default gateway to prove the local network works, then ping a public IP address to prove traffic reaches the internet. If that works but names fail, I run nslookup. If it cannot resolve the name, the problem is DNS. If a public IP is unreachable, tracert shows the hop where replies stop. The limit is that many firewalls drop ICMP. A failed ping or asterisks in tracert do not prove a device is down, so I confirm with another test before I blame hardware.
rubricPoints: States what ipconfig/ifconfig reveals: IP address, subnet mask, gateway and DNS, and that 169.254 means DHCP failed.
Uses ping to test reachability, moving from the gateway to a public IP.
Uses tracert to locate the hop where traffic stops.
Uses nslookup to separate DNS failures from connectivity failures.
Notes that blocked ICMP can make ping or tracert fail on healthy devices.

suggested.rationale: The skill is reading command output in a troubleshooting scenario and choosing the next test, which exam-style worked situations practice better than any current mission.

lessons.plain: Cables and connectors are the plugs and wires that let parts of a computer talk to each other and to the outside world. Each kind has its own shape so it only fits where it belongs, like keys cut for specific locks. HDMI and DisplayPort carry picture and sound to a screen. USB-A and USB-C connect accessories and can supply power. RJ-45 is the plug on a wired network cable. SATA connects drives inside the case. Recognising each one by its shape, and knowing what it carries, lets you pick the right cable and plug it in without forcing or damaging anything.
lessons.guessPrompt: A monitor's port looks like a rectangle with one corner cut off at an angle, and a small latch on the cable clicks when you push it in. Is it more likely made for sound and pictures, for network traffic, or for a storage drive, and why do you think the corner is cut?
lessons.teach:
A connector is the shaped plug or socket at the end of a cable; a port is the socket it fits into. Most connectors are keyed, meaning shaped so they fit only one way, which prevents wrong or upside-down insertion.

HDMI (High-Definition Multimedia Interface) is a flat, wide plug with slanted sides that carries digital video and audio, common on TVs, monitors and game consoles. DisplayPort carries the same kinds of signal but is shaped as a rectangle with one corner cut off and usually has a locking latch; it is common on PC monitors and graphics cards. USB (Universal Serial Bus) connects peripherals, meaning add-on devices such as keyboards, and can deliver power. USB-A is the classic flat rectangle that fits one way only; USB-C is a small rounded oval that is reversible, fitting either way up. RJ-45 is the eight-wire clear plastic plug with a springy clip used on Ethernet cables, which are twisted-pair copper cables for wired networking. SATA (Serial ATA) connects internal drives: a thin L-shaped 7-pin data connector runs to the motherboard, and a wider L-shaped 15-pin connector brings power from the power supply.

Worked example: a user adds a 2.5-inch SATA SSD and a new monitor. Step one, connect the thin L-shaped SATA data cable from the drive to a motherboard SATA port, matching the L. Step two, connect the wide L-shaped SATA power plug from the power supply. Step three, the monitor has a cut-corner port, so use a DisplayPort cable into the graphics card. Step four, plug the RJ-45 cable in until the clip clicks.

A common mistake is assuming every USB-C port does everything. The shape is identical, but one port may carry only data while another also carries video or fast charging, depending on the device. Another mistake is forcing a keyed plug the wrong way, which can bend pins and leave a drive or display that the system never detects.

questions.prompt: A community library is setting up a public kiosk PC. Step 1: the keyboard's flat rectangular plug fits only one way, so it goes into a USB-A port. Step 2: the wired network uses an Ethernet cable, so its eight-wire clear plastic RJ-45 plug is pushed into the network port until the clip clicks. Step 3: the wall-mounted TV that will show the kiosk screen has only one input, a flat, wide port with slanted sides that must carry both picture and sound. Which cable should be used for Step 3?
choices: A DisplayPort cable, because it is the PC monitor standard and carries video and audio
An HDMI cable, because the flat, wide port with slanted sides is an HDMI port
A USB-C cable, because every USB-C port can carry video to a display
A thin L-shaped SATA data cable, because it carries digital signals from the PC
questions.why: A flat, wide port with slanted sides is the HDMI shape, and HDMI carries digital video and audio to TVs.

questions.prompt: A technician says a connector is 'keyed.' What does that mean?
choices: It is shaped so it can fit into its port only one way
It can be inserted either way up, like a reversible plug
It carries both power and data on the same set of pins
It has a locking latch that must be pressed before removal
questions.why: Keyed means the connector's shape lets it fit only one way, which prevents wrong or upside-down insertion.

questions.prompt: At a small accounting firm, a technician installs a new internal SATA drive in a workstation. The power supply's plug is connected, but the computer never detects the drive. The technician notices the thin L-shaped data plug was pushed in hard against resistance and some pins look bent. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The drive needs an RJ-45 cable to be recognised by the system
The keyed data plug was forced the wrong way, damaging the connection
SATA drives only work when connected through a USB-C port
The wide 15-pin power plug should have gone to the motherboard
questions.why: Forcing a keyed plug the wrong way can bend pins and leave a drive the system never detects.

questions.prompt: A designer's laptop has two USB-C ports that look exactly alike. An external monitor shows a picture when plugged into the left port but nothing when plugged into the right port. What best explains this?
choices: The right port is plugged in upside down, so it is not reversible
The ports share a shape, but only one of them carries video
The monitor needs an RJ-45 cable to receive a video signal
USB-C can never carry video, so the left port must really be HDMI
questions.why: USB-C ports have an identical shape, but depending on the device one may carry only data while another also carries video.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell HDMI, DisplayPort, USB-A, USB-C, RJ-45 and SATA apart by shape and purpose, and name one limit of judging a cable only by how its plug looks.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with what the cable is for, then check the shape. HDMI and DisplayPort both carry video and audio to a screen: HDMI is flat with slanted sides, while DisplayPort is a rectangle with one corner cut off and usually a latch. USB-A is the flat rectangle that goes in one way only; USB-C is the small rounded oval that fits either way. RJ-45 is the clear eight-wire plug with a clip on an Ethernet network cable. Inside the case, SATA uses a thin L-shaped data plug to the motherboard and a wider L-shaped power plug from the power supply. These shapes are keyed, so if a plug resists, I flip it rather than push harder. The limit is that shape does not tell you capability: two USB-C ports look identical, but one may not output video or fast charging, so I check the device's port labelling or specs.
rubricPoints: Matches HDMI and DisplayPort to video and audio and distinguishes them by shape.
Distinguishes USB-A as one-way and USB-C as reversible.
Identifies RJ-45 as the clipped plug on Ethernet network cable.
Describes SATA data and SATA power as separate L-shaped internal connectors.
Explains keying and that plugs should never be forced.
Names a limit, such as identical USB-C plugs having different capabilities.

suggested.rationale: No existing mission or planned engine handles physical connectors, and the exam tests this through short situations where you match a device or port description to the right cable, so reasoning through such scenarios adds the most.

lessons.plain: A motherboard is the main circuit board inside a computer that every other part plugs into. The processor, the chip that does the computing, has to fit a specific mount on that board, much like a key has to fit one particular lock. The board also has a support controller that decides which processors and features it can handle. Add-on cards, such as a graphics card or a network card, slide into long slots on the board to add abilities. Building or upgrading a PC means checking that these pieces fit physically and are designed to work together, then installing them carefully.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a brand-new processor and a motherboard whose processor mount looks the same shape. Do you think that alone guarantees the computer will start? What else might need to match?
lessons.teach:
A motherboard is the main circuit board everything connects to. The CPU (central processing unit, the chip that runs instructions) sits in a socket, a physical mount whose pin layout fits only one CPU family. Intel desktop sockets use LGA (land grid array: pins in the socket, flat pads on the chip). AMD's older AM4 used PGA (pin grid array: pins on the chip), while AM5 uses LGA. The chipset is the board's support controller; it decides which CPU generations, how many USB and storage connections, and whether overclocking are supported. Form factor is the board's size and screw-hole pattern: ATX (full size), microATX (smaller, fewer slots), mini-ITX (smallest, usually one expansion slot). Add-on cards go in PCIe (Peripheral Component Interconnect Express) slots, named by lane count: x1, x4, x8, x16. A card fits a slot its own size or larger.

Compatibility is a chain: the CPU must match the socket, the chipset must support that CPU generation, and the firmware (BIOS or UEFI, the startup software stored on the board) must be new enough to recognize it.

Worked example: a customer wants a Ryzen 7000-series CPU in a small case. Step 1: Ryzen 7000 uses AM5, so AM4 boards are ruled out. Step 2: choose an AM5 chipset such as B650. Step 3: the case takes microATX, so ATX is ruled out. Step 4: the graphics card needs an x16 slot, which the board has. Install: wear an antistatic wrist strap, line up the triangle mark on the CPU with the socket's mark, lower it without pressure, close the retention arm, apply thermal paste (a heat-transfer compound) and fit the cooler, put standoffs (spacers that keep the board off the metal case) in place, mount the board, then seat the card and screw down its bracket.

Common mistake: assuming a matching socket means guaranteed compatibility. A board with an older chipset or outdated firmware may fail POST (power-on self-test): fans spin but nothing appears on screen. Forcing a misaligned CPU bends pins and can ruin the board.

questions.prompt: Harbor Street Library wants to put a newer-generation CPU into one of its existing desktops instead of buying a new board. A technician works through the compatibility chain. Step 1: the new CPU's socket matches the socket already on the board. Step 2: the board's chipset is listed as supporting that newer CPU generation. Step 3: ??? Step 4: wearing an antistatic wrist strap, the technician removes the old CPU, aligns the triangle mark on the new chip with the socket's mark, lowers it without pressure, closes the retention arm, then applies fresh thermal paste and refits the cooler. Which step 3 completes the chain?
choices: Confirm the board's firmware (BIOS/UEFI) is new enough to recognize the newer CPU, and update it if it is not
Replace the board with an ATX model so the newer CPU has enough room around the socket
Remove the standoffs so the board sits closer to the case and the new cooler fits
Move the graphics card from its x16 slot to an x1 slot to free up power for the newer CPU
questions.why: Compatibility is a chain of socket, chipset and firmware, and with the first two links confirmed, the remaining risk is firmware too old to recognize the newer CPU, which would cause a failed POST.

questions.prompt: An accounting office wants to add a storage controller card that has an x8 PCIe connector. The motherboard's free slots are one x1, one x4 and one x16. Which free slot can take the card?
choices: The x16 slot, because a card fits a slot its own size or larger
None of them, because an x8 card only fits an x8 slot
The x1 slot, because any PCIe card fits any PCIe slot
The x4 slot, because it is the closest size to x8
questions.why: A PCIe card fits a slot with the same or a higher lane count, so an x8 card fits the x16 slot but not the smaller x1 or x4 slots.

questions.prompt: A technician at a small print shop installs a CPU whose socket matches the motherboard. On power-up the fans spin, but nothing ever appears on the screen. Based on the compatibility chain, what is the most likely cause?
choices: The PCIe graphics card is in an x16 slot, which is too large for it
The board's chipset is too old or its firmware is outdated for that CPU, so it fails POST
The thermal paste was applied, which blocks the CPU from making contact with the socket
The board is microATX, and microATX boards cannot show video during POST
questions.why: A matching socket does not guarantee compatibility; an older chipset or outdated firmware can leave the board unable to run the CPU, so it fails POST with fans spinning and no display.

questions.prompt: While pulling an old AMD CPU out of an AM4 motherboard at a community college lab, a technician sees rows of pins on the underside of the chip itself. What does this tell the technician?
choices: The CPU uses PGA (pins on the chip), so the pins can bend if it is forced or dropped
The CPU uses LGA (pins in the socket), so the chip's flat pads need no special care
The pins prove the CPU will also fit an AM5 board, since both are AMD sockets
The pins mean the chipset, not the socket, decides whether the CPU physically fits
questions.why: AM4 uses pin grid array, with pins on the chip, and those pins bend if the CPU is forced or mishandled. AM5 is a different LGA socket, so an AM4 chip will not fit it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would confirm a CPU, motherboard, and graphics card will work together for a build, and name one limit of checking only the socket type.
lessons.modelAnswer: I check compatibility as a chain. First, the CPU's socket has to match the board's socket, for example AM5 for a Ryzen 7000 chip, because the pin layout is physically different between families. Second, the chipset has to support that CPU generation, since the chipset controls which processors and features the board allows. Third, the board's firmware, the BIOS or UEFI, must be recent enough to recognize the CPU. Then I check the form factor fits the case, like microATX for a small case, and that there is a PCIe slot at least as large as the card, usually x16 for graphics. The limit of checking only the socket is that a board can share the socket yet have an older chipset or old firmware, so the PC powers on but fails POST with no display until the BIOS is updated.
rubricPoints: The CPU socket must physically match the motherboard socket.
The chipset must support the specific CPU generation.
Firmware (BIOS/UEFI) may need an update to recognize a newer CPU.
Board form factor must fit the case and add-on cards need a PCIe slot of equal or larger size.
A matching socket alone does not guarantee the system will POST.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine involves PC hardware, so reasoning through exam-style build scenarios that rule out incompatible parts best builds this skill.

lessons.plain: RAM (random access memory) is the computer's short-term workspace: it holds the programs and data the processor is using right now, and it empties when power is off. RAM comes in generations, such as DDR4 and DDR5, and each motherboard accepts only one generation. Think of it like a phone charger plug: two plugs can look nearly identical, but only the right shape fits the socket. Placement matters too. Put two matching sticks in the right slots and the processor can use two lanes to memory at once, called dual-channel, instead of one lane, called single-channel.
lessons.guessPrompt: A friend has a computer whose motherboard takes DDR4 memory, and they found a cheap DDR5 stick of the same size and capacity. Do you think it will work if they push it into the slot hard enough? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A memory module is a small circuit board covered in RAM chips. In desktops it is called a DIMM (dual inline memory module). In laptops it is a smaller SO-DIMM (small outline DIMM). DDR stands for double data rate, meaning data moves on both the rising and the falling edge of each clock tick. The number after it is the generation.

DDR4 and DDR5 desktop DIMMs both have 288 pins. Their notch, the gap in the gold contact edge, sits in a different place. The notch is a physical key, so the wrong generation will not seat. They also differ electrically. DDR4 runs at about 1.2 volts. DDR5 runs at about 1.1 volts and carries its own power-management chip on the module. DDR5 also splits each module into two smaller independent subchannels, which raises speed. A board supports exactly one generation, so check the motherboard specification first.

A memory channel is an independent data path between the memory controller and the slots. Dual-channel means two channels work in parallel, which roughly doubles memory bandwidth (data moved per second). Single-channel uses just one path.

Worked example: a board has four DDR5 slots labeled A1, A2, B1 and B2, and the user has two matched 16 GB sticks. Step 1: confirm the board is DDR5. Step 2: read the manual, which says to use A2 and B2 for two sticks; these slots are often color-coded. Step 3: power off, unplug the system, and wear an anti-static wrist strap. Step 4: open the slot latches, line up the notch, and press straight down until the clips click. Step 5: boot and confirm in firmware setup that 32 GB is shown, running in dual-channel.

Common mistake: putting both sticks in neighboring slots such as A1 and A2. Both then share one channel, and the system runs single-channel. Mixed modules run at the slowest stick's speed. The consequence is a working but noticeably slower system, especially when graphics are built into the processor and borrow system RAM.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm is upgrading an office desktop. Its board has four DDR4 slots labeled DIMM1, DIMM2, DIMM3 and DIMM4, and the manual says DIMM1 and DIMM2 are on channel A while DIMM3 and DIMM4 are on channel B. The technician has two matched 8 GB DDR4 sticks and wants the fastest result. Step 1: the board specification confirms it supports DDR4, so the sticks are the right generation. Step 2: ??? Step 3: the technician powers off, unplugs the PC, and puts on an anti-static wrist strap. Step 4: the slot latches are opened, each notch is lined up, and each stick is pressed straight down until the clips click. Step 5: firmware setup shows 16 GB running in dual-channel. What is Step 2?
choices: Choose DIMM1 and DIMM2, because neighboring slots let the two sticks share one fast path
Choose one slot from channel A and one from channel B, such as DIMM2 and DIMM4
Choose any two slots, because all four slots connect to the same memory controller
Choose DIMM3 and DIMM4, because the slots farthest from the processor give the best speed
questions.why: Dual-channel needs one stick on each independent channel, so placing one stick in a channel A slot and the other in a channel B slot lets both paths work in parallel.

questions.prompt: A school IT volunteer tries to install a DDR5 desktop DIMM into a motherboard built for DDR4. Both have 288 pins, but the stick will not go into the slot. What is the reason?
choices: The notch sits in a different place, which physically keys each generation to its own slot
DDR5 modules only fit laptop SO-DIMM slots, not desktop slots
DDR5 sticks need more force because they have more pins than DDR4
The slot latches only open once firmware detects a DDR5 module
questions.why: DDR4 and DDR5 DIMMs have the same pin count, but their notches are in different positions, so a stick of the wrong generation cannot seat.

questions.prompt: A home user adds one DDR4 stick rated 2666 to a PC that already has one DDR4 stick rated 3200. The PC boots and shows the extra memory. At what speed will the memory most likely run?
choices: 3200, because the faster stick sets the pace for both
Each stick runs at its own rated speed independently
Somewhere halfway between, about 2933
2666, because mixed modules run at the slowest stick's speed
questions.why: When modules are mixed, the memory runs at the speed of the slowest stick, which here is the one rated 2666.

questions.prompt: A design studio's new PC uses graphics built into the processor and feels sluggish. Firmware setup shows the correct total memory but reports single-channel. The two matched sticks are in slots A1 and A2 on a board with slots A1, A2, B1 and B2. What is the best fix?
choices: Replace both sticks with DDR5 modules of the same size
Add an anti-static strap and reseat both sticks in the same slots
Swap the two sticks between A1 and A2
Move one stick to a channel B slot so each channel has one stick
questions.why: Sticks in A1 and A2 share one channel, so moving one to a B slot puts a stick on each channel and enables dual-channel, roughly doubling bandwidth that the built-in graphics also borrows.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose and install RAM for an upgrade, covering why DDR4 and DDR5 are not interchangeable and how slot placement affects performance. Name at least one limit or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I check what the motherboard supports, because a board takes only one memory generation. DDR4 and DDR5 DIMMs both have 288 pins, but the key notch sits in a different spot, so the wrong one physically won't seat. They also differ electrically: DDR5 runs at lower voltage, has its own power-management chip, and splits each module into two subchannels. Next, for performance I install a matched pair in the slots the manual names for dual-channel, often A2 and B2, which are usually color-coded. That gives two parallel paths to memory and roughly doubles bandwidth. If both sticks share one channel, the system still works but runs single-channel and slower. One tradeoff is that mixing modules is possible, but everything drops to the slowest stick's speed, so a matched kit is safer. I power down, unplug, use an anti-static strap, and then verify capacity and channel mode in firmware.
rubricPoints: States that a motherboard supports only one generation, DDR4 or DDR5, and the two are not interchangeable.
Mentions the different notch position as the physical key, plus at least one electrical difference such as voltage.
Explains that dual-channel uses two parallel memory paths and increases bandwidth.
Identifies installing matched sticks in the manual's specified slots, and that the wrong slots cause single-channel.
Names a tradeoff or limit, such as mixed modules running at the slowest speed.
Includes safe installation and verification steps such as ESD protection and checking firmware.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine covers physical memory installation, so reasoning through exam-style upgrade scenarios about generation and slot choice builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Storage devices are where a computer keeps files when the power is off. A hard disk drive (HDD) spins magnetic platters like a record player, so it is cheap and roomy but slow. A solid-state drive (SSD) uses memory chips with no moving parts, so it is much faster. SSDs connect either through SATA, an older and slower link, or through NVMe, a newer and much faster one. RAID combines several drives so they act as one. Depending on how it is set up, RAID can make storage faster, help it survive a dead drive, or do both. Think of it as a team of drives sharing the work.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose every file you save is copied to two drives at the same moment. If one drive dies, what happens to your files, and what did you give up to get that protection?
lessons.teach:
An HDD (hard disk drive) stores data magnetically on spinning platters. Its speed is partly set by RPM (revolutions per minute), usually 5,400 or 7,200. HDDs are cheap per gigabyte but slow. An SSD (solid-state drive) stores data in flash memory chips and has no moving parts, so it is far faster and tougher. SATA (Serial ATA) is an interface that tops out near 600 MB/s. A 2.5-inch SATA SSD needs a SATA data cable and a SATA power cable. NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) is a faster method that runs SSDs over PCIe, the motherboard's high-speed lanes, and reaches several thousand MB/s. NVMe drives usually use M.2, a small stick screwed directly into the board. Some M.2 slots accept only SATA or only NVMe, so check the motherboard manual first.

RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) groups drives into one volume. RAID 0 (striping) splits data across drives for speed but has no redundancy, so one failure loses everything. RAID 1 (mirroring) copies the same data to two drives, giving half the total space and surviving one failure. RAID 5 needs at least three drives and spreads parity across them. Parity is calculated recovery data that rebuilds a lost drive. RAID 5 costs one drive's worth of space and survives one failure. RAID 10 stripes across mirrored pairs and needs four drives. It gives speed plus redundancy at half capacity.

Worked example: an office file server has four 4 TB drives and must survive a failure with maximum space. RAID 0 is out because it has no redundancy. RAID 1 or RAID 10 yields 8 TB. RAID 5 yields (4−1)×4 = 12 TB and survives one failure, so RAID 5 fits.

A common mistake is treating RAID as a backup. A deleted or encrypted file vanishes from every mirror instantly. When a drive dies, the array keeps running degraded. A second failure before you replace the drive can lose all data. Also, a new drive must be initialized, partitioned and formatted before the operating system shows it.

questions.prompt: A small design studio has three 2 TB drives for a shared project volume. The volume must keep working if one drive fails, and the studio wants as much usable space as possible. Step 1: RAID 0 is ruled out because striping has no redundancy. Step 2: RAID 10 is ruled out because it needs four drives and only three are available. Step 3: RAID 1 mirrors data onto two drives, so it gives only 2 TB. Step 4: ??? Step 5: RAID 5 is chosen. Which statement correctly completes Step 4?
choices: RAID 5 works with three drives and yields (3 − 1) × 2 = 4 TB while surviving one failure
RAID 5 yields 4 TB and survives any two drive failures because parity is on every drive
RAID 5 yields half of 6 TB = 3 TB, the same cost as mirroring
RAID 5 yields 3 × 2 = 6 TB, because parity is spread out and takes up no space
questions.why: RAID 5 needs at least three drives, gives up one drive's worth of space to parity (recovery data), and survives one failure, so it provides 4 TB here, more than RAID 1's 2 TB.

questions.prompt: A technician buys an NVMe M.2 SSD and screws it into the only M.2 slot on a customer's motherboard. The system does not detect the drive. The motherboard manual says that slot supports SATA M.2 drives only. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The slot cannot run NVMe, which uses PCIe lanes, so this drive needs an NVMe-capable M.2 slot
The drive needs a SATA power cable connected before it will appear
NVMe drives always require a SATA data cable alongside the M.2 connection
The drive must first be set up in RAID 0 before a single M.2 slot will detect it
questions.why: M.2 is only a physical form factor. NVMe runs over PCIe, and a SATA-only M.2 slot cannot talk to an NVMe drive, which is why you check the manual first.

questions.prompt: A clinic's records server uses RAID 5 across four drives. One drive fails, and the server keeps running. The manager plans to wait a few months before replacing the drive because 'everything still works.' What is the main risk of waiting?
choices: The array immediately converts to RAID 0 and runs faster until a replacement is added
The array is running degraded, and a second drive failure before the replacement could lose all data
None, because RAID 5 rebuilds the failed drive's data onto the remaining drives permanently
The usable space doubles while degraded, which can fill the remaining drives
questions.why: RAID 5 survives only one failure. While degraded it has no redundancy left, so a second failure can destroy the whole volume.

questions.prompt: A technician installs a brand-new 1 TB SATA SSD in a desktop and connects both the SATA data cable and the SATA power cable. The drive is physically working, but it does not appear as a usable drive letter in the operating system. What should the technician do next?
choices: Add a second drive and create a RAID 1 mirror, because single SSDs are hidden by default
Swap the drive for an HDD, because SATA is limited to about 600 MB/s and cannot run an SSD
Replace the SATA data cable with an M.2 adapter, since SATA SSDs cannot be read without one
Initialize the drive, create a partition, and format it so the operating system can use it
questions.why: A new drive must be initialized, partitioned, and formatted before the operating system will show it as a usable volume.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a SATA SSD, an NVMe SSD and an HDD, and between RAID 0, 1, 5 and 10. Name one tradeoff and one thing RAID does not protect against.
lessons.modelAnswer: For speed I pick an SSD, because it has no moving parts. NVMe runs over PCIe and is several times faster than SATA, which caps near 600 MB/s. I would still check that the motherboard's M.2 slot supports NVMe. HDDs win on cheap bulk capacity. For RAID, the tradeoff is speed, safety and usable space. RAID 0 stripes data for speed but loses everything if one drive fails. RAID 1 mirrors two drives and gives up half the space. RAID 5 needs three or more drives and loses one drive's worth of space to parity, but survives one failure. RAID 10 needs four drives and gives speed plus redundancy at half capacity. RAID is not a backup. Deletions and ransomware hit every copy at once, and a degraded array is at risk until the failed drive is replaced.
rubricPoints: HDDs are cheap and large but slow, while SSDs are fast because they have no moving parts.
NVMe uses PCIe and is much faster than SATA, and M.2 slot support must be checked.
RAID 0 gives speed with no redundancy, and RAID 1 mirrors at half capacity.
RAID 5 needs three or more drives and uses parity to survive one failure.
RAID 10 needs four drives and combines speed with redundancy.
RAID is not a backup, and a degraded array should be repaired quickly.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine builds PCs, and the exam tests this through scenarios like choosing a drive type or RAID level for a stated need, so reasoning through such situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: A power supply is the box inside a computer that turns the electricity from the wall outlet into the steady, lower voltages the parts need. Picking one means two checks. Is it strong enough, measured in watts? Does it have the right plugs for every part? Cooling is the other half. Every chip turns some of its power into heat, and that heat has to be carried away or the chip slows down or shuts off. Think of it like a car. The power supply is the fuel line, and it must deliver enough fuel through the right fittings. Cooling is the radiator that keeps the engine from overheating.
lessons.guessPrompt: A processor draws about 125 watts, a graphics card draws about 300 watts, and everything else in the PC draws about 75 watts. Would you buy a 500-watt power supply, a 650-watt one, or a 1,600-watt one, and why?
lessons.teach:
A power supply unit (PSU) converts wall AC power into the low DC voltages, mainly 12 V, 5 V and 3.3 V, that the parts use. Choose one on two things.

The first is wattage, the most power the PSU can deliver continuously. Add up what the parts draw, then leave headroom of roughly 20 to 30 percent so the PSU is not running flat out. The second is connectors, which must match the parts. A 24-pin ATX connector feeds the motherboard. A 4-pin or 8-pin EPS connector feeds the CPU. Graphics cards take 6-pin or 8-pin PCIe connectors, or the newer 16-pin 12VHPWR (12V-2x6) connector. SATA power connectors feed drives. An 80 Plus rating (Bronze, Gold, Platinum) describes efficiency, meaning how little power is wasted as heat. It does not add wattage.

Cooling removes heat. A CPU's TDP (thermal design power) is roughly the heat, in watts, its cooler must handle. An air cooler pairs a metal heatsink with a fan. An all-in-one (AIO) liquid cooler pumps liquid to a radiator with fans, which suits high-TDP chips. Passive cooling uses a heatsink alone and fits only low-power systems. Thermal paste fills the microscopic gaps between the CPU and the cooler. Case fans should pull air in at the front and push it out the back or top.

Worked example: the CPU draws 125 W, the graphics card 300 W, and everything else about 75 W, for a total of 500 W. Adding 25 percent gives 625 W, so pick a 650 W unit. The card needs two 8-pin PCIe plugs, so confirm the PSU has them. A 125 W CPU needs a solid tower air cooler or an AIO, not a slim low-profile cooler.

A common mistake is buying a PSU that exactly matches the total, or forgetting the graphics card connectors. Under heavy load the PC may reboot or power off without warning. An undersized cooler, or missing thermal paste, makes the CPU throttle, which means it slows itself down to cool off, and it may shut down if it stays too hot.

questions.prompt:
A small design studio orders a workstation. Its CPU draws 65 W, its graphics card draws 200 W, and the motherboard, drives, RAM and fans together draw about 55 W. A technician sizes the power supply unit (PSU), the part that turns wall AC power into the DC voltages the parts use.

Step 1: Add the draws: 65 + 200 + 55 = 320 W.
Step 2: Leave about 25 percent headroom so the PSU is not running flat out: ______
Step 3: Round up to the next common size and pick a 450 W unit. Then confirm the PSU has the PCIe power connectors the graphics card needs.

Which completes Step 2?
choices: 320 W is enough because it already covers every part, so headroom is optional.
320 W + 25 W = 345 W, so the target is 345 W.
320 W × 1.25 = 400 W, so the target is at least 400 W.
320 W × 2 = 640 W, so the target is 640 W.
questions.why: Headroom is a percentage of the total draw, and 25 percent of 320 W is 80 W, which makes a 400 W target that rounds up to a 450 W unit.

questions.prompt: While building a PC, a technician sees an 8-pin power socket on the motherboard next to the CPU socket. This socket supplies power only to the processor. Which PSU cable belongs in it?
choices: An 8-pin EPS connector, which is the CPU power connector
A SATA power connector, which feeds drives
The 24-pin ATX connector, which feeds the whole motherboard
An 8-pin PCIe connector, because it has the same number of pins
questions.why: The EPS connector, in a 4-pin or 8-pin form, is the one meant to feed the CPU. PCIe connectors are for graphics cards, even when they have the same pin count.

questions.prompt: A school IT lab is building PCs whose parts add up to about 480 W of continuous draw. Which PSU is the best fit?
choices: 500 W, 80 Plus Platinum
480 W, 80 Plus Gold
650 W, 80 Plus Bronze
550 W, 80 Plus Gold
questions.why: Adding 20 to 30 percent headroom to 480 W gives a target of roughly 576 to 624 W, and only the 650 W unit meets it. An 80 Plus rating describes efficiency, meaning how little power is wasted as heat, and it does not add wattage.

questions.prompt: A user reinstalled their CPU cooler after cleaning it. Since then, the PC slows down sharply a few minutes into video rendering and once shut itself off. The cooler is rated well above the CPU's TDP (thermal design power, roughly the heat in watts the cooler must remove), and the fans spin normally. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The PSU's 80 Plus rating is too low for rendering work.
The SATA power cable to the storage drive is slightly loose.
No thermal paste was applied between the CPU and the cooler when it was reinstalled.
The case fans pull air in at the front and push it out the back.
questions.why: Without thermal paste to fill the microscopic gaps between the CPU and the cooler, heat does not transfer well. The CPU then throttles, meaning it slows itself down to cool off, and it can shut down if it stays too hot.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate is speccing a new workstation and plans to buy the cheapest power supply whose wattage equals the parts' total, plus the smallest cooler that fits. In your own words, explain how you would choose the PSU and the cooling instead, and name one tradeoff, such as headroom versus cost or air versus liquid cooling.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I'd add up what each part draws: the CPU, the graphics card, and roughly the rest of the system. Then I'd add about 20 to 30 percent headroom, because a PSU running at its limit can make the PC reboot under heavy load. Next I'd check the connectors: a 24-pin for the motherboard, an 8-pin EPS for the CPU, the right PCIe or 16-pin plugs for the graphics card, and SATA power for the drives. 80 Plus Gold is about efficiency, not extra watts. For cooling, I'd match the cooler to the CPU's TDP, use thermal paste, and set the case fans for front-to-back airflow. The tradeoff is cost. Extra headroom and a big cooler cost more up front. An AIO handles high heat well but adds a pump that can fail, while a good tower air cooler is simpler but bulkier.
rubricPoints: Sums component power draw and adds roughly 20 to 30 percent headroom.
Checks connectors: 24-pin motherboard, 4/8-pin CPU, PCIe or 16-pin GPU, SATA for drives.
Explains that 80 Plus measures efficiency, not capacity.
Matches cooler capacity to CPU TDP and mentions thermal paste and airflow.
Names the consequence of undersizing: shutdowns, reboots or thermal throttling.
States a real tradeoff such as cost versus headroom or air versus liquid cooling.

suggested.rationale: No OpsForge mission or planned engine covers PC hardware, so working through exam-style build scenarios that require sizing wattage, matching connectors and picking a cooler is the most useful practice.

lessons.plain: A peripheral is any device that plugs into a computer to add a job it cannot do alone. A printer puts documents on paper, a scanner turns paper into a digital file, and a multifunction device (MFD) combines printing, scanning, copying, and sometimes faxing in one box. Installing one means connecting it, giving the computer the right translator software, and setting it up so people can use it safely. Maintaining it means keeping that software current and the settings correct. Think of a new office coffee machine. Someone has to plug it in, put it where everyone can reach it, set the defaults, and keep it working.
lessons.guessPrompt: An office printer works fine all week, but on Monday nobody can print to it, even though it is powered on and shows no errors. What might have changed about how the computers find it on the network?
lessons.teach:
Installing a printer, scanner, or MFD comes down to three things: connection, driver, and configuration. The connection is how the device reaches computers. Options are USB for one local PC, wired Ethernet or Wi-Fi so it sits on the network, or Bluetooth for short-range mobile use. A driver is software that translates what an application wants to print into commands the device understands. Common printer languages include PCL (Printer Command Language) and PostScript, and the driver must match both the device model and the computer's operating system and 32-bit or 64-bit version. Configuration means the default settings: paper tray, size, orientation, duplex (printing on both sides), color or grayscale, and quality. For scanners and MFDs it also covers where scans go, such as an email address, a shared network folder, or a cloud storage service. A flatbed is the glass plate for single pages. An ADF (automatic document feeder) pulls in a stack of pages.

Worked example: you add a network MFD for a team. First, cable it to the switch. Second, give it a fixed address, either set by hand or as a DHCP reservation (a rule telling the address-handing server to always give this device the same address). Third, install the correct driver on a print server, a computer that holds the shared queue, so users connect to the share. Fourth, set defaults such as duplex and grayscale to save supplies. Fifth, set up scan-to-folder with an account that has permission to write to that folder. Then print and scan a test page.

A common mistake is leaving the device on a changing, DHCP-assigned address. When the address changes, every PC points at an empty spot and printing stops for the whole office. Maintenance also includes firmware updates (the device's built-in software), keeping drivers current, and security features. These include user badging or PIN release, so jobs print only when the owner is present, and audit logs that record who printed what.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic's front-desk laser printer sits on the office network. On Monday, none of the four reception PCs can print. A technician works through it. Step 1: she checks a reception PC and sees its print queue points to the printer at 192.168.20.45. Step 2: she prints a configuration page from the printer's own control panel, which shows its current address is 192.168.20.61. Step 3: she concludes the printer had been getting a changing address from the DHCP server (the server that hands out addresses automatically), and that address has changed, so every PC is pointing at an empty spot. Step 4: ______. Step 5: she points the queues at the fixed address and prints a test page from each PC. What is the missing Step 4?
choices: Update the printer's firmware so it keeps the same address after a restart
Reinstall the printer driver on all four PCs, because a driver mismatch caused the failure
Switch the printer to Bluetooth so the PCs no longer depend on an address
Give the printer a fixed address, by hand or as a DHCP reservation so it always gets the same one
questions.why: The failure came from a changing DHCP-assigned address, so the fix is a fixed address (set by hand or reserved in DHCP) that will not move again.

questions.prompt: A technician at an architecture firm downloads a driver for a new plotter-style printer and installs it on a designer's workstation, but the install fails. A driver is the software that translates what an application wants to print into commands the device understands. Which pair of things must the driver match?
choices: The network switch model and the Wi-Fi band in use
The printer language only, either PCL or PostScript, regardless of operating system
The printer's paper size and the default tray
The device model and the computer's operating system, including whether it is 32-bit or 64-bit
questions.why: A driver must match both the specific device model and the computer's operating system and its 32-bit or 64-bit version.

questions.prompt: A small accounting office worries that client tax forms sit in the shared printer's output tray where anyone walking by can pick them up. Which printer feature most directly solves this?
choices: Adding an automatic document feeder (ADF)
User badging or PIN release, so a job prints only when its owner is at the device
Giving the printer a DHCP reservation
Setting the default to duplex and grayscale
questions.why: Badging or PIN release holds each job until the owner authenticates at the printer, so confidential pages are not left unattended.

questions.prompt: At a property management company, the multifunction device (MFD, a single unit that prints, scans, and often copies) is set up to scan to a shared network folder. Printing works, but every scan-to-folder attempt fails with an access error. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The account the MFD uses for scan-to-folder does not have permission to write to that folder
The scan is being made on the flatbed instead of the ADF
The printer driver on the print server is the 32-bit version
The default orientation is set to landscape instead of portrait
questions.why: Scan-to-folder needs an account with write permission on the destination folder; without it the device cannot save the file there, even though printing still works.
