Notes that RAID is not a backup and that the failed drive must be identified correctly before a rebuild.
Verifies the fix and documents it.

suggested.rationale: No existing mission covers drive hardware, boot order or RAID, so reasoning through exam-style symptom scenarios best builds the habit of matching each symptom to a cause and testing it.

lessons.plain: When a computer is switched on, its built-in startup software runs a quick health check of the most basic parts before it loads the operating system. If something vital such as the processor, memory or power is wrong, the machine signals the fault with beeps, small lights, or a two-digit code. Troubleshooting the motherboard, the processor and the power supply means reading those signals and using simple test tools to find which part has failed. It works like a car dashboard. A warning light does not fix anything, but it tells you where to look first, so you are not guessing and swapping random parts.
lessons.guessPrompt: A PC's fans spin and its lights come on, but nothing appears on screen, and it gives one long beep followed by two short beeps. Is the power supply likely to be completely dead? What would you check before buying any parts?
lessons.teach:
POST (power-on self-test) is the check that the firmware runs every time a PC starts. Firmware is the BIOS or UEFI, the startup program stored on the motherboard. POST checks the CPU (processor), the RAM (memory) and the video output. If POST cannot finish, the firmware reports the fault in one of three ways. Beep codes are patterns of short and long beeps. Diagnostic LEDs are small labelled lights on the board, for example CPU, DRAM, VGA and BOOT. POST codes are two-digit hexadecimal numbers. They appear on a built-in debug display or on a POST card, which is an add-in card that reads and shows the code where startup stopped.

This works because POST tests parts in a fixed order. The last code shown, or the first lit LED, points at the stage that failed.

Worked example. A PC has fans spinning, a black screen and one long beep followed by two short beeps. First, the fans spinning tells you the PSU (power supply unit) delivers at least some power. The PSU converts wall AC into steady DC voltages of about 3.3, 5 and 12 volts. Second, you look up the beep pattern in the motherboard manual, and it means a video fault. Third, you reseat the graphics card and test it again, and the PC passes POST. Fourth, you write down what you found and what fixed it.

When there is no power at all, use a PSU tester or a multimeter to confirm the voltages are within about 5 percent of their targets. A multimeter is a meter that measures voltage. Other clues point to specific parts. A clock that keeps resetting suggests a dead CMOS battery, the coin cell that keeps firmware settings. Swollen capacitors or a burning smell suggest board or PSU damage. Shutdowns under load suggest CPU overheating, often from dried thermal paste or a failed cooler.

A common mistake is treating beep codes as universal. Each firmware vendor uses different patterns, so the same beeps can mean different faults on different boards. Misreading them leads you to replace good parts, spend money for nothing, and leave the real fault in place.

questions.prompt: A workstation at a dental clinic will not start properly. Its fans spin and the screen stays black. It makes no beeps. The motherboard has diagnostic LEDs labelled CPU, DRAM, VGA and BOOT, and the DRAM light stays lit. Step 1: The spinning fans show that the PSU (power supply unit) is delivering at least some power. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: The technician reseats the memory modules and powers on again, and the PC passes POST (power-on self-test). Step 4: The technician records the symptom, the lit LED and the fix. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Look up the pattern in a general beep code chart, because the same beeps mean the same fault on every board
Read the lit DRAM LED as the stage where POST stopped, which points at the memory
Replace the CPU, because the processor is always the first part POST checks
Replace the PSU, because a black screen shows the power supply is not delivering the correct voltages
questions.why: POST tests parts in a fixed order, so the lit DRAM LED marks the memory stage as the place where startup failed, and that justifies reseating the RAM next.

questions.prompt: A technician at a print shop fits a POST card into a PC that will not boot. A POST card is an add-in card that reads and displays POST codes. The card shows a two-digit hexadecimal code and then stops changing. What does that last code tell the technician?
choices: It shows the voltage the PSU is currently supplying
It gives the age of the CMOS battery in months
It points at the stage of POST where startup stopped
It is the number of beeps the firmware will sound next
questions.why: POST runs its checks in a fixed order, so the last code shown identifies the stage that failed.

questions.prompt: A technician tests a power supply with a multimeter, a meter that measures voltage. A healthy reading should be within about 5 percent of its target. Which reading is outside that range?
choices: 12 V rail reading 11.7 V
3.3 V rail reading 3.25 V
12 V rail reading 12.4 V
5 V rail reading 4.6 V
questions.why: Five percent of 5 V is 0.25 V, so the acceptable range is about 4.75 to 5.25 V, and 4.6 V falls below it. The other readings are all inside their ranges.

questions.prompt: A PC at a warehouse office gives three short beeps at startup. A junior technician looks up the pattern in a beep chart printed for a different motherboard maker. Based on that chart, they replace the RAM, but the PC still fails. What is the most likely reason?
choices: Three short beeps always mean a dead CMOS battery on every board
RAM faults can only be shown on diagnostic LEDs, never by beeps
Firmware vendors use different beep patterns, so the chart may describe a different fault
Beep codes only appear when the PSU is completely dead
questions.why: Beep codes are not universal. Using another vendor's chart can lead you to replace a good part and leave the real fault in place, so the pattern should be checked in that board's own manual.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use POST signals and a simple meter to narrow down a PC that will not start. Include one limit of relying on beep codes or POST codes.
lessons.modelAnswer: When a PC is powered on, the BIOS or UEFI firmware runs POST. POST checks the CPU, the memory and the video in a fixed order. If it stops, the firmware tells me where it stopped through beeps, labelled board LEDs, or a two-digit code on a debug display or POST card. First I decide whether this is a power problem or a POST problem. If nothing spins at all, I test the power supply with a PSU tester or multimeter to check that its 3.3, 5 and 12 volt outputs are within tolerance. If the fans spin but the PC halts, I read the signal, look it up in that board's manual, and reseat or swap only the part it points to. One limit is that codes are not standard across vendors, so I must use the right manual. Another is that a code shows where startup stopped, not always the root cause. A bad PSU or a short circuit can make a healthy part look faulty.
rubricPoints: Defines POST as the firmware's startup check of CPU, memory and video.
Names the signal types: beep codes, diagnostic LEDs, and POST codes shown on a display or POST card.
Separates no-power faults from POST-halt faults and uses a PSU tester or multimeter for the power side.
Looks up codes in the specific motherboard or firmware manual before acting.
States a limit: codes are vendor-specific and show where startup stopped, not always the root cause.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine simulates PC hardware, so reasoning through exam-style symptom scenarios, matching beeps, LEDs and voltages to a likely failed part, builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Network trouble usually shows up in one of three ways. Intermittent connectivity means the connection keeps dropping and coming back. Slow transfer speeds mean it stays connected but data crawls. Limited connectivity means the device reaches the local network but not the internet. Think of a phone line. A crackly line that cuts out is intermittent. A clear line where the other person speaks very slowly is slow. A line that only reaches people inside your own building is limited. Naming the symptom correctly is the first clue to where the fault is, whether that is a cable, a radio signal, or a missing address.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your laptop shows it is connected to the office network, but no websites load. Its network address starts with 169.254. What do you think went wrong: is the laptop broken, or did it fail to get something from the network?
lessons.teach:
Network faults fall into three symptom groups.

Intermittent connectivity means the link works, drops, then returns. On wired links, suspect a damaged or loose cable or a failing switch port. On wireless links, suspect a weak signal caused by distance or walls. Also suspect interference, meaning other radio sources such as microwaves, cordless phones, or nearby access points using the same channel. A channel is the slice of the radio band an access point transmits on.

Slow transfer speeds mean the link stays up but moves data slowly. One cause is a duplex mismatch. Duplex describes whether a link sends and receives at once (full) or takes turns (half). If the two ends disagree, collisions slow everything. Other causes are a port that negotiated a lower speed, a crowded Wi-Fi channel, or an old wireless standard.

Limited connectivity means the device reaches the local network but nothing beyond it. Often it never got an IP address (its network address) from DHCP, the service that hands out addresses automatically. Windows then gives itself an APIPA address beginning 169.254, which can only talk to neighbours using the same kind of address.

Splitting faults this way works because each symptom points to a different cause, so you can narrow your theory before you change anything.

Worked example: a user reports "connected, no internet." First, run ipconfig, the Windows command that shows the address settings. It shows 169.254.10.5 and no default gateway, which is the router leading off the local network. Your theory is that DHCP failed. To test it, check the link light, reseat the cable, and run ipconfig /release then /renew. The address is still 169.254. Next, plug a known-good laptop into the same wall jack. It also fails, so the PC is not the problem. Fix or escalate the switch port or DHCP server. Then verify the PC gets a normal address and can ping a website. Ping sends a small test message and waits for a reply. Finally, document what you found and did.

A common mistake is replacing the network card or reinstalling drivers first. A 169.254 address usually means no DHCP reply arrived, so the fault is often upstream. In a busy office, one bad port or DHCP server can cut off many users, so asking whether others are affected comes early.

questions.prompt: At a small architecture firm, a designer says copying a 2 GB drawing file to the office file server over a wired connection takes far longer than it used to. The link light stays on and the connection never drops. Step 1 (identify): the link stays up but moves data slowly, so this is a slow-transfer problem, not intermittent or limited connectivity. Step 2 (theorize): a duplex mismatch is likely. Step 3 (test): the PC's network settings show half duplex while the switch port is set to full duplex, so the two ends disagree. Step 4 (plan and implement): set both ends to the same duplex setting. Step 5: ???. Step 6 (document): record the mismatch and the setting change. What belongs in Step 5?
choices: Run ipconfig /release and /renew to get a fresh address from DHCP
Copy the same 2 GB file again and confirm it now transfers at normal speed
Move the PC closer to the wireless access point to strengthen the signal
Replace the PC's network card so the new card negotiates duplex correctly
questions.why: After implementing the fix, you verify it by repeating the action that showed the symptom and confirming that normal speed has returned, then you document.

questions.prompt: A laptop at a community library shows it is connected to the network, but no websites load. ipconfig shows the address 169.254.77.20. What does this address most likely tell you?
choices: The two ends of the link disagree on duplex, so collisions are slowing traffic
The laptop's Wi-Fi is on a crowded channel and is transferring data slowly
The laptop got no reply from DHCP and gave itself an address that only reaches neighbours using the same kind of address
The laptop received a normal address and the website itself is down
questions.why: A 169.254 (APIPA) address means Windows assigned itself an address because no DHCP reply arrived, which gives limited connectivity.

questions.prompt: At a food warehouse, handheld scanners on Wi-Fi keep dropping and reconnecting, but only in the corner next to the staff break room, and mostly at lunchtime. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Radio interference from a microwave oven in the break room
A duplex mismatch on the switch port that serves the scanners
The DHCP server has run out of addresses for the scanners
The scanners are using an old wireless standard, which makes them slow all day
questions.why: Drops that happen only near the break room at lunchtime point to interference, meaning another radio source such as a microwave disrupting the Wi-Fi signal.

questions.prompt: At an insurance office, one employee reports no internet access, and her PC shows a 169.254 address. The technician immediately reinstalls the network card driver, and nothing changes. What should the technician have done early instead?
choices: Replaced the network card, because a driver reinstall is never enough
Set the PC to half duplex, because a mismatch stops DHCP replies
Changed the Wi-Fi channel, because a crowded channel causes 169.254 addresses
Asked whether other users were affected, because the fault is often upstream at a switch port or the DHCP server
questions.why: A 169.254 address usually means no DHCP reply arrived, so the fault is often upstream, and checking whether others are affected narrows the theory before anything is changed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell apart intermittent, slow, and limited connectivity, and what each one points to. Include one limit of relying on a 169.254 address as your clue.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by naming the symptom. If the connection drops and returns, it is intermittent. On a wired link, I check for a loose or damaged cable or a bad switch port. On Wi-Fi, I check signal strength and interference from other devices or access points on the same channel. If the connection stays up but transfers are sluggish, it is slow. Then I look at duplex mismatches, a port that negotiated a low speed, crowded channels, or an old wireless standard. If the device reaches the local network but not the internet, it is limited. I run ipconfig, and a 169.254 address with no gateway tells me DHCP never answered. That clue has limits, though. It tells me DHCP failed, not why. The cause could be the cable, the switch port, or the DHCP server itself. And a device with a valid address can still show limited connectivity because of a wrong gateway or DNS. So I test with a known-good device before blaming the PC.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes intermittent, slow, and limited connectivity by their symptoms.
Names likely wired causes (cable, switch port, duplex) and wireless causes (signal, interference, channel).
Explains that a 169.254 APIPA address means the device got no DHCP reply.
Notes that the APIPA clue does not pinpoint the failing component, so further testing is needed.
Uses a comparison test, such as a known-good device, before replacing hardware.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine simulates office cable, Wi-Fi, and DHCP faults, so working through exam-style symptom scenarios builds the diagnostic reasoning best.

lessons.plain: When a computer or network link breaks, guessing wastes time. A few simple hand tools let you measure instead of guess. A multimeter reads electricity: how much voltage is present and whether a wire is unbroken. A loopback plug makes a port talk to itself, so you can see whether the port works. A cable tester checks every wire inside a network cable. A POST card plugs into a motherboard and shows a code for how far the computer got while starting up. Think of them as a doctor's thermometer and stethoscope: each answers one question.
lessons.guessPrompt: A desk's network link light stays off. You have a plug that makes the computer's network port talk to itself, and a device that checks each wire in the cable. Which would you use first, and what would each result tell you?
lessons.teach:
Each tool answers one narrow question, which is why they speed up troubleshooting.

A multimeter is a handheld meter that measures voltage (electrical pressure, in volts), resistance (opposition to current, in ohms), and continuity (whether an unbroken path exists, often shown with a beep). Technicians use it to check that a power supply unit (PSU, the box that converts wall power into the lower voltages a PC uses) outputs about 12, 5 and 3.3 volts, or that a wire is not broken.

A loopback plug is a small connector that routes a port's transmit pins back to its receive pins. Software sends data out and checks that the same data comes back. If it does, the port and its network interface card (NIC, the hardware that connects a PC to a network) are working.

A cable tester has two ends you attach to each end of a network cable. It checks each of the eight wires for opens (breaks), shorts (wires touching) and miswiring (wires in the wrong order).

A POST card is an expansion card that displays two-digit hexadecimal codes during POST, the Power-On Self-Test the firmware runs to check hardware at startup. The last code shown tells you which stage failed, even with no display.

Worked example: a user has no network link. Step one, put a loopback plug in the PC's port; the link light comes on and the test passes, so the NIC is fine. Step two, run the cable tester on the patch cable; wire 6 shows open. Step three, replace the cable; the link comes up. Each test removed one suspect.

Common mistake: measuring resistance or continuity on a powered circuit, or leaving the meter on the wrong setting. This gives false readings and can blow the meter's fuse or damage components. Also remember a basic cable tester proves wiring, not that the cable can carry full speed.

questions.prompt:
At a small bakery, the office PC's fans spin when it is switched on, but the monitor stays black and nothing else happens. The technician works through it one suspect at a time.

Step 1: With the PC switched on, the technician sets a multimeter to DC voltage and probes the PSU's output connector. The readings are 12.1 V, 5.0 V and 3.3 V, all close to normal, so the power supply is ruled out.

Step 2: ???

Step 3: The motherboard manual says the last code shown belongs to the memory-check stage. The technician reseats the RAM sticks, and the PC boots normally.

Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Install a POST card, power the PC on, and note the last two-digit code it displays
Attach a cable tester to both ends of the monitor cable and check all eight wires
Put a loopback plug in the PC's network port and run the send-and-receive test
Set the multimeter to continuity and probe the motherboard while the PC is running
questions.why: A POST card shows the startup codes even when there is no display, and the last code shown points to the stage that failed, which is exactly what Step 3 relies on.

questions.prompt: At a print shop, a workstation will not connect to the network. A technician wants to find out whether the PC's own network port and network interface card (NIC) work, without involving the wall jack or any cable. Which tool answers that question directly?
choices: A cable tester, which checks the eight wires for breaks, shorts and wrong order
A POST card, which shows the firmware's startup codes on a small display
A multimeter set to voltage, which reads the 12, 5 and 3.3 volt outputs
A loopback plug, which sends the port's outgoing signal back into its receive pins
questions.why: A loopback plug tests only the port and NIC: if the data the software sends comes back unchanged, that hardware is working, and no cable is involved.

questions.prompt: A trainee at a repair shop wants to check whether a PC's power cable has a break inside it. The trainee leaves the cable plugged in and powered, sets the multimeter to continuity, and touches the probes to it. What is the most likely result?
choices: An accurate reading, because continuity checks work the same on any circuit
A false reading, and possibly a blown meter fuse or damaged components
No reading at all, because continuity can only be tested on network cables
A reading in volts, because the meter switches modes on its own when it detects power
questions.why: Continuity and resistance must be measured with the circuit unpowered; doing it on a live circuit gives false readings and can blow the meter's fuse or damage parts.

questions.prompt: At a law office, a technician runs a basic cable tester on a new patch cable. All eight wires pass, with no opens, shorts or miswiring. However, the PC connected with that cable only ever links at a much lower speed than expected. What does the passing test actually prove?
choices: That the switch port at the far end is configured properly
That the cable can carry the network's full rated speed
That the wires are connected end to end in the correct order
That the PC's network interface card is working correctly
questions.why: A basic cable tester proves the wiring is correct (no breaks, shorts or wrong order), not that the cable can carry full speed, so the slow link still needs investigating.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a multimeter, loopback plug, cable tester and POST card each tell you, and name one limit of at least one of these tools.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each tool answers a single yes-or-no style question so I can rule out one part at a time. A multimeter measures voltage, resistance and continuity; I use it to confirm a power supply puts out the right voltages or that a wire is unbroken, but only in continuity or resistance mode with the power off. A loopback plug sends a port's output straight back into its input, so a pass means the port and network card work, which points me at the cable or beyond. A cable tester checks each wire in a network cable for breaks, shorts and wrong order. A POST card shows startup codes from the Power-On Self-Test, so I can see where boot stops even with no screen. The limit: a simple cable tester proves the wiring is correct but not that the cable can actually run at full speed, and a loopback pass says nothing about the switch.
rubricPoints: States that a multimeter measures voltage, resistance and continuity, such as checking power supply outputs.
Explains that a loopback plug feeds a port's output back to its input to prove the port or NIC works.
Explains that a cable tester checks individual wires for opens, shorts and miswiring.
Explains that a POST card shows startup codes indicating where the Power-On Self-Test stopped.
Names a real limit or safety point, such as no resistance tests on live circuits or basic testers not proving speed.

suggested.rationale: No OpsForge mission handles physical tools, so reasoning through exam-style symptom scenarios to pick the right tool and read its result is the most useful practice.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Logistics: A Laptop Upgrade and a Struggling Phone
scenarios.scenario:
You are the new desktop support technician at Brightwater Logistics, a fictional delivery company. A dispatcher named Priya brings you her work laptop and her company phone with three complaints.

First, the laptop is slow when she opens many browser tabs. The laptop's spec sheet says it has two SODIMM slots. A SODIMM (small outline dual inline memory module) is the short, laptop-sized stick of RAM. RAM (random access memory) is the fast, temporary working memory a computer uses for open programs. One slot holds an 8 GB DDR4-3200 SODIMM and the other slot is empty. DDR4 and DDR5 are two different generations of RAM. They use different notch positions and different voltages, so one generation will not fit or work in a slot built for the other. Priya has already bought a 16 GB DDR5 DIMM from a shop. A DIMM (dual inline memory module) is the longer RAM stick made for desktop computers.

Second, she wants more storage space. The spec sheet lists one free M.2 2280 slot marked "SATA only." M.2 is a small, card-shaped connector for internal drives. The number 2280 means the card is 22 mm wide and 80 mm long. SATA (Serial ATA) is an older and slower way for a drive to talk to the computer. NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) is a newer, much faster method that sends data over PCIe lanes, which are high-speed data paths on the motherboard. An NVMe drive and an M.2 SATA drive can look almost the same and share the same M.2 shape, but a slot that supports only SATA cannot use an NVMe drive. Priya bought a 1 TB M.2 2280 NVMe drive.

Third, her phone has two problems. Its battery now lasts only about four hours, and the back of the phone feels warm even while it sits in her pocket. You open the phone's battery usage screen. It shows that a route-mapping app used 48% of the battery in the last 24 hours, almost all of it in the background, meaning while the app was not on screen. That app's location permission is set to "Always." No other app is above 8%. The phone has no cracks or swelling. Separately, her work email has not synced since yesterday morning. Syncing means the phone exchanging new data with the company's mail server. Brightwater uses MDM (mobile device management), which is company software that installs a settings package called a profile onto the phone. The profile sets up the work email account. The MDM console shows that Priya's profile is installed and in good standing. On the phone, the status bar shows an airplane icon next to a Wi-Fi icon. Priya says she switched on airplane mode during a flight yesterday and then turned Wi-Fi back on to use the plane's internet. Airplane mode is a setting that switches off all of the phone's radios, including cellular data. You are now standing in the warehouse, where no Wi-Fi network is available to the phone.

1. Explain whether the RAM Priya bought will work in her laptop, and state exactly what RAM module she should get instead.
2. Explain whether the NVMe drive will work in the free M.2 slot, and state what drive she should get.
3. Identify the most likely cause of the short battery life and the warmth, and describe the fix.
4. Identify why work email is not syncing, describe the fix, and name one step you should not take.
modelAnswer: The RAM she bought will not work, for two reasons. First, it is a DIMM. A DIMM is the longer desktop-sized stick, and it physically will not fit a laptop's SODIMM slot. Second, it is DDR5, and the laptop uses DDR4. The two generations have different notch positions and voltages, so they are not interchangeable. She should get a DDR4 SODIMM, ideally DDR4-3200 to match the 8 GB stick already installed, and install it in the empty slot. A matching 8 GB DDR4-3200 SODIMM is the safest choice. A different size of DDR4-3200 SODIMM is acceptable as long as the laptop's spec sheet supports that amount. Forcing the wrong module in could damage the slot or the stick.

The NVMe drive will not work. Even though it has the correct M.2 2280 shape, the slot is marked SATA only. A SATA-only slot cannot talk to an NVMe drive, so the laptop would not detect it. She should get an M.2 2280 SATA drive. The common mistake is to judge compatibility by physical size alone. Size and shape are not enough: the drive's interface, SATA or NVMe, must match what the slot supports.

The most likely cause is the route-mapping app running in the background with location set to Always. That setting keeps the GPS and processor busy even when the app is not in use. This drains the battery quickly and produces heat. The battery usage screen confirms it: the app used 48% of the battery, mostly in the background, and no other app is above 8%. Because there is no swelling or damage, a failing battery is not the first suspect. To fix it, change the app's location permission to While Using (or Never if it is not needed for work), restrict or turn off its background activity, and close the app. Then check battery life and temperature over the next day. Replacing the battery first would be guessing and would not remove the real cause.

Airplane mode is still on, so cellular data is off. Priya turned Wi-Fi back on during the flight, but in the warehouse there is no Wi-Fi, so the phone has no network connection at all and cannot sync. To fix it, turn airplane mode off so that cellular data returns, confirm that cellular data is enabled, then open email or trigger a manual sync and check that new messages arrive. Do not remove or reinstall the MDM profile. The console shows the profile is installed and healthy, so removing it would not help. Removing it could also delete the work email account and its settings until the phone is enrolled in MDM again.

scenarios.title: No Network at the Front Desk: Harbor Lane Bookkeeping
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Lane Bookkeeping is a fictional five-person office. It has one SOHO router, meaning a small office/home office router: a single box that connects the office to the internet and hands out addresses to local devices. The router uses DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol), a service that automatically gives each device an IP address (its network address), a subnet mask (which tells the device which addresses are local), and a default gateway (the router address the device sends internet traffic to). The router's own local address is 192.168.10.1, and every other PC in the office gets an address that starts with 192.168.10.

Each desk has a wall jack. Inside the wall, the cable runs to a patch panel in the back closet. A patch panel is a row of ports where in-wall cables end, so short patch cables can connect them to the switch. A switch is a box that connects wired devices on the same local network.

This morning the new front-desk PC, which uses a wired connection, cannot reach the internet or the shared printer. You open a command prompt and run ipconfig, a Windows command that shows the PC's current network settings. It reports IPv4 Address 169.254.37.112, Subnet Mask 255.255.0.0, and a blank Default Gateway. You then run ping 192.168.10.1. Ping sends small test messages to an address and reports whether replies come back. Every attempt fails with no reply. The network port light on the PC is off.

You plug the wall cable into a cable tester. A cable tester is a handheld tool that sends a signal down each of the eight wires and shows which wires are connected end to end. The cable follows T568B, a standard wire-color order. The tester shows wires 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, and 8 passing, but wires 3 and 6 show as open, meaning not connected. At the patch panel, you see that the wires for that port were pushed into the panel's metal slots by hand rather than seated properly.

The owner also asks for two more changes. First, outside clients must be able to reach a secure upload web page hosted on the office server at 192.168.10.20. The page uses HTTPS, which is encrypted web traffic. Second, the owner wants a guest Wi-Fi network for visiting clients. A Wi-Fi analyzer, a tool that shows nearby wireless networks and the channels they use, shows the 2.4 GHz band crowded with eleven neighbouring networks. The 5 GHz band has only two. All office and guest devices are less than three years old.

1. Explain what the ipconfig and ping results tell you about the front-desk PC, and why.
2. Using the cable tester result, identify the most likely fault and the specific tool and action that fixes it.
3. Describe the router rule needed so outside clients can reach the upload page, including the port number and protocol, and one setting on the server that keeps the rule working.
4. Recommend the frequency band and the wireless security setting for the guest network, and justify both choices.
subParts: Diagnose and fix the cabling fault
Choose guest Wi-Fi band and encryption
modelAnswer: An address starting with 169.254 is an APIPA address. APIPA stands for Automatic Private IP Addressing. Windows assigns one to itself when it asks for a DHCP address and gets no answer. The blank default gateway confirms that the PC never received settings from the router. The failed ping to 192.168.10.1 shows the PC cannot reach the router at all. Two things point to the physical connection rather than a settings problem: the network port light is off, and the other PCs get normal 192.168.10.x addresses, so the DHCP service is working. The PC's request is simply not reaching the router. A common mistake is to type in a static (manually entered) address or to reboot the router. Neither fixes a broken link, and a static address can hide the real fault.

Wires 3 and 6 are open. In T568B, 10/100 Ethernet uses pins 1, 2, 3, and 6, with 1 and 2 sending and 3 and 6 receiving. With one required pair broken, the link cannot come up, which explains both the dark port light and the missing DHCP address. The likely cause is the badly seated wires at the patch panel. The fix is to re-terminate that port with a punchdown tool. This tool pushes each wire fully into its slot (called an IDC, or insulation-displacement contact) and trims the excess wire, following the T568B color order. Afterwards, re-run the cable tester to confirm all eight wires pass. Then run ipconfig again: expect a 192.168.10.x address and a gateway of 192.168.10.1. Finally, confirm that ping to 192.168.10.1 succeeds. A crimper is the wrong tool here, because it attaches RJ45 plugs to cable ends, not wires to a patch panel.

Create a port forwarding rule on the router. Port forwarding tells the router to send traffic that arrives at its public internet address on a chosen port to one specific inside device. This is needed because NAT (Network Address Translation) lets every office device share one public address, and NAT drops unexpected incoming traffic unless a rule says where it should go. The rule is: incoming TCP port 443 (HTTPS) goes to internal address 192.168.10.20, port 443. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is the connection-based protocol that HTTPS uses. On the server side, give it a static IP address, or create a DHCP reservation so it always receives 192.168.10.20. Otherwise DHCP could hand the server a different address later, and the rule would point at the wrong device or at nothing, so clients would lose access. Forward only port 443. Do not also open ports such as 3389 (RDP, Remote Desktop Protocol) to the internet, because that exposes the server to attack.

Use the 5 GHz band. The Wi-Fi analyzer shows 2.4 GHz crowded with eleven networks, which causes interference and slow speeds. 5 GHz is nearly empty and has more non-overlapping channels and higher throughput. Its shorter range is acceptable inside a small office. All devices are less than three years old, so they should support 5 GHz. For security, choose WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3). It is the newest standard and resists password-guessing attacks better than WPA2 because it uses SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), a safer way for a device and the router to prove they share the password. If any guest device cannot connect, a WPA2/WPA3 mixed (transition) mode is a fallback, or WPA2 with AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) encryption. Never use open or WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy, an old, easily broken standard) security. Keep guests on a separate guest network or VLAN (virtual LAN, a setting that splits one physical network into isolated groups) so visitors cannot reach the office server or printer.

scenarios.title: Building a Video-Editing Workstation at Brightwater Studio
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Studio is a small, fictional video production company. Its editor, Priya, needs a new workstation, and your lead has handed you a motherboard plus a bin of spare parts. Your job is to pick parts that fit together and explain why you rejected the others.

The motherboard is the main circuit board that every other part plugs into. This one uses the AM5 socket. A socket is the physical mount that holds the CPU, the processor that runs instructions. A CPU only fits and works in the socket it was designed for. The board's chipset, the controller chip that decides which features and memory types the board supports, accepts DDR5 memory only. DDR5 is a generation of RAM, the short-term working memory a computer uses while it runs. The board has four RAM slots, labelled A1, A2, B1 and B2. The manual says that when you install two modules, they go in A2 and B2. The board also has two M.2 slots that support NVMe. M.2 is a small, stick-shaped drive format, and NVMe is a fast way for a drive to talk to the CPU over PCIe lanes, which are high-speed data paths on the board. Finally, it has four SATA ports. SATA is an older, slower drive connection that uses a thin data cable plus a separate power cable. The board's built-in RAID supports RAID 0, RAID 1 and RAID 10. RAID is a way of combining several drives so they act as one, either for speed or for protection against a drive failing.

The parts bin holds the following. CPU X is an AM5 processor drawing about 120 W (watts, a measure of power). CPU Y is a cheaper AM4 processor drawing about 105 W. Kit A is two 16 GB DDR4-3200 modules. Kit B is two matched 16 GB DDR5-5600 modules. There is also one single 32 GB DDR5-5600 module. For storage there is one 1 TB NVMe M.2 SSD (a solid-state drive, with no moving parts) and two identical 4 TB SATA HDDs (hard disk drives, which store data on spinning platters). The graphics card draws about 285 W and needs two 8-pin PCIe power connectors. There are two PSUs to choose from. A PSU, or power supply unit, converts wall power into the voltages the parts use. PSU 1 is rated at 550 W and has a 24-pin motherboard connector, one 8-pin CPU connector and one 8-pin PCIe connector. PSU 2 is rated at 850 W and has a 24-pin motherboard connector, one 8-pin CPU connector and two 8-pin PCIe connectors. Your lead estimates that the motherboard, RAM, drives and fans together draw about 100 W.

Priya's requirements are simple. The operating system and editing software should load as fast as possible. Her project files should survive if one hard drive dies. Memory should run in dual-channel mode. Dual-channel means two matched modules work side by side, so the CPU can move data to and from memory roughly twice as wide at once.

1. Choose the CPU and explain why you rejected the other one.
2. Choose the RAM and the slots you will use, and explain why each of the other two memory options does not meet the requirements.
3. Decide where the operating system goes and which RAID level to use for the two hard drives. Explain your choice, and say why RAID 0 and RAID 10 are wrong here.
4. Choose the PSU. Show your wattage estimate and check the connectors.
subParts: RAM selection and dual-channel slot placement
Boot drive and RAID level choice
modelAnswer: Choose CPU X. The motherboard has an AM5 socket, and CPU X is an AM5 processor, so it physically fits and the chipset supports it. CPU Y is an AM4 processor. A socket is built for one pin layout, so an AM4 CPU will not seat in an AM5 socket at all. On top of that, this board and chipset only work with DDR5, while AM4 is a DDR4-era platform. Being cheaper does not matter if the part cannot be installed. Forcing a CPU into the wrong socket can bend pins or damage the board.

Choose Kit B, the two matched 16 GB DDR5-5600 modules, and install them in slots A2 and B2 as the manual directs. That gives 32 GB running in dual-channel mode. Kit A is DDR4. DDR4 and DDR5 modules have their notch in different places, and the chipset supports DDR5 only, so DDR4 will not fit and cannot work. The single 32 GB DDR5 module is the right type and gives the same total capacity. However, one module can only run in single-channel mode, so Priya would lose the dual-channel bandwidth she asked for. A common mistake is putting two modules in neighbouring slots such as A1 and A2. That can leave the memory in single-channel mode, or out of the board's recommended layout, so always follow the manual's slot order.

Install the operating system and editing software on the 1 TB NVMe M.2 SSD. NVMe uses fast PCIe lanes and has no moving parts, so it boots and loads programs much faster than the SATA hard drives. Put the two 4 TB SATA HDDs in RAID 1, which is mirroring: every file is written to both drives. If one drive fails, the other still holds a full copy. You get 4 TB of usable space and can replace the failed drive and rebuild the mirror. RAID 0 is striping, which splits data across both drives for speed with no redundancy. If either drive in a RAID 0 set dies, the whole set is lost, which is the opposite of what Priya needs. RAID 10 needs at least four drives, and only two are available. Also note that RAID 1 protects against a drive failing, but it is not a backup. A deleted or corrupted file is deleted or corrupted on both drives at once, so the studio still needs separate backups.

Choose PSU 2, the 850 W unit. The estimate is CPU 120 W + graphics card 285 W + about 100 W for the board, RAM, drives and fans, which comes to about 505 W. A PSU should have headroom, meaning spare capacity above the estimated load, commonly around 20 to 30 percent or more. That headroom covers short power spikes and lets the PSU run cooler and more efficiently. Adding 20 to 30 percent to 505 W gives roughly 600 to 660 W, so 550 W is too tight, while 850 W is comfortable and leaves room for later upgrades. The connectors also have to match. PSU 2 has the 24-pin motherboard connector, the 8-pin CPU connector, and the two 8-pin PCIe connectors the graphics card needs. PSU 1 has only one 8-pin PCIe connector, so it cannot power the graphics card properly even before you consider wattage. An undersized PSU can cause random shutdowns or crashes under heavy load, such as when Priya renders video.

scenarios.title: Hollyridge Veterinary Clinics: Sorting Workloads Between a Laptop VM and the Cloud
scenarios.scenario:
Hollyridge Veterinary Clinics is a fictional chain of four animal hospitals. You have just joined its two-person IT team, and your manager, Dana, hands you four requests to sort out this week.

Request A comes from Priya, the office manager. Her 16 GB, 4-core Windows laptop must run an old dosage-calculator program that only works on an older operating system. She installed a type 2 hypervisor, which is a program that runs on top of a normal operating system and lets you create virtual machines (VMs). A VM is a software-made computer with its own operating system, sharing the real (host) machine's hardware. She created one VM and gave it 14 GB of RAM (memory) and all 4 CPU cores. Now the VM starts, but the whole laptop, host and VM alike, freezes and crawls.

Request B: staff need email, shared calendars and a word processor. Nobody on the team wants to install, patch or back up any servers or software for this.

Request C: a contractor has written an online appointment-booking web app. Bookings are quiet most of the year but jump roughly tenfold during spring vaccination season. The contractor wants to upload the code and not manage operating systems, patching or server sizing. Dana also wants to pay only for what is actually used.

Request D: by company policy, the patient-records database must stay on servers inside Hollyridge's own building. The public website and the booking app from Request C can run in a public cloud, meaning shared infrastructure owned by an outside provider and rented to many customers. The two sides must be connected so the booking app can check patient records.

Your tasks:
1. Explain why Priya's laptop freezes and say how you would reallocate the VM's resources. Also explain why a type 2 hypervisor, rather than a type 1, is the right choice for her laptop.
2. Choose the cloud service model for Request B. Explain why it fits and why the near-miss model does not.
3. Choose the cloud service model for Request C. Name the cloud characteristics that cover the seasonal spike and the pay-for-use billing, and explain why IaaS is the near-miss that does not fit.
4. Name the cloud deployment model that fits Request D and explain why neither a purely public nor a purely private cloud matches the policy.
subParts: Fix the VM's resource allocation; type 1 vs. type 2 hypervisor
Service model for email and office apps
Service model and cloud characteristics for the booking app
Deployment model for split records and website
modelAnswer:
The VM and the host share one pool of physical hardware. Priya gave the VM 14 of the laptop's 16 GB of RAM and all 4 cores, so the host operating system was starved. It had about 2 GB left for Windows plus the hypervisor itself, and it had to compete for every core. Because the host is the thing actually running the hypervisor, a starved host drags the VM down with it, so both freeze.

The fix is to shut the VM down and lower its allocation, leaving the host comfortable headroom. For example, give the VM about 4 GB of RAM (6 GB at most) and 1-2 virtual CPUs, which still leaves the host roughly 10-12 GB and 2-3 cores. An old calculator program and an older operating system need very little. Size the VM to the workload, not to the maximum the hardware has. As a step-by-step check: 16 GB total, minus 4 GB for the VM, leaves 12 GB for the host, so neither side is starved.

A type 2 hypervisor runs as an ordinary application on top of an existing operating system. That fits Priya, who still needs Windows and her normal apps on the laptop and only occasionally needs the old program. A type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor installs directly on the hardware in place of a normal operating system. It suits dedicated servers that run many VMs, and it would replace her everyday Windows setup, so it is the wrong fit for a personal work laptop.

The right model is SaaS (Software as a Service). The provider delivers finished, ready-to-use applications over the internet, here email, calendars and a word processor. The provider runs and patches everything underneath: servers, storage, operating systems and the application itself. Hollyridge just signs in and uses the software, which matches the requirement that nobody installs, patches or backs up servers or software.

The near-miss is PaaS (Platform as a Service). PaaS gives you a managed platform for running applications that you write or deploy yourself. Hollyridge has no app to build here. It needs finished office software, so PaaS would leave the team building or deploying something it simply wants to consume. IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) misses even further, because the team would then have to manage operating systems and install and patch the email software itself.

The right model is PaaS (Platform as a Service). The provider manages the hardware, operating systems, patching and runtime environment, meaning the software the code needs in order to run. The contractor only uploads and manages the application code, which is exactly what was asked for.

The seasonal tenfold spike is handled by rapid elasticity. This is the cloud's ability to add capacity quickly and automatically when demand rises, then shrink it again when demand falls. It works because of resource pooling: the provider keeps a large shared pool of hardware serving many customers, so extra capacity is always available to hand out. Paying only for what is used is metered utilization. The provider measures consumption, such as compute time, storage and traffic, and bills by actual use, so the quiet months cost less than vaccination season.

IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) is the near-miss. It does run in the cloud and can scale. However, it rents you raw virtual servers, storage and networking, and you are responsible for the operating system, its patching and the server sizing. That breaks the contractor's requirement not to manage operating systems, patching or server sizing. SaaS does not fit either, because SaaS is finished software, not a place to run your own custom booking app.

The right model is a hybrid cloud. A hybrid cloud combines a private cloud, meaning computing resources used by one organization only and here kept in its own building, with a public cloud, connected so that data and applications can work together across both. In this case the patient-records database stays on Hollyridge's own on-site servers, as the policy requires. The website and booking app run in the public cloud, and the link between the two lets the booking app check records.

A purely public cloud would break the policy, because the records would leave the building. A purely private cloud would satisfy the policy but would give up the public cloud's elasticity and metered billing for the website and the seasonal booking spike. Hollyridge would then have to buy and run enough of its own hardware to cover peak season all year round. A community cloud, which is shared by several organizations with common needs, also does not match, because nothing in the request involves sharing infrastructure with other organizations.

scenarios.title: No Network After a Desk Move at Harbor Lane Supply
scenarios.scenario:
You are the new junior support technician at Harbor Lane Supply, a small fictional wholesaler of bakery equipment. On Monday morning, Dana from accounting calls: her desktop PC cannot reach the shared drive or any websites. Every other PC in the office is working normally.

When you arrive, you see Dana's desk was moved across the room over the weekend. The PC connects to a wall jack through a patch cable, which is a short network cable that runs from the computer to the wall. The cable now runs across the floor, under the wheels of her office chair. On the back of the PC, the link light is off. The link light is a small LED next to the network port that glows when the port detects a working electrical connection at the other end. The port belongs to the NIC (network interface card), the hardware in the PC that connects it to a wired network.

You run ipconfig, a Windows command that shows the PC's network settings. The PC's IP address, its numeric address on the network, starts with 169.254. That range is an APIPA address. APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing) means Windows gave itself a fallback address because it could not reach the DHCP server. A DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) server is the device that normally hands out working addresses automatically. A PC with an APIPA address has what is called limited connectivity: it may talk to nearby devices that also have APIPA addresses, but it cannot reach the rest of the network or the internet.

Your toolkit has two relevant tools. The first is a loopback plug, a small connector that plugs into a network port and sends the port's outgoing signal straight back into it, so you can test the port by itself. The second is a cable tester, a two-piece device that checks every wire inside a network cable for breaks or wrong connections.

Your lead reminds you to follow the standard troubleshooting methodology. In order, it is: identify the problem, establish a theory of probable cause, test the theory, establish a plan of action and implement it, verify full system functionality, and document the findings.

1. Identify the problem. Name the specific things you should do or ask before you form any theory, and say which fact in this scenario matters most.
2. Establish and test a theory. State the most probable cause. Then explain how you would use the loopback plug and the cable tester to test it, and what each result would tell you.
3. Suppose the cable tester shows a break in one of the wires. Describe your plan, how you implement it, and how you verify the fix, including one step that stops the problem from coming back.
4. Document. List what your ticket notes should record, and explain why skipping this step causes trouble later.
modelAnswer: Start by gathering information before guessing at a cause. Question the user: when did it stop working, did it ever work at this desk, are there any error messages, and has anything changed? Find out what changed recently. Check whether the problem can be reproduced, and confirm its scope. Here, only Dana's PC is affected, and every other PC works. That points to something local to her setup, not the DHCP server or the internet connection. If you will be making changes, back up important data or confirm it is safe first. The most important fact is the recent change: the desk was moved over the weekend, and the cable now lies under chair wheels. Recent changes are a top source of new faults. A common mistake is jumping straight to a fix, such as reinstalling the network driver, without asking what changed.

The most probable cause is physical damage to the patch cable, or a loose cable, from the move. The evidence is the link light being off, which means there is no electrical connection at the port. The APIPA address fits this too: with no connection, the PC cannot reach the DHCP server, so Windows gives itself a fallback address. Start with the simplest checks: reseat the cable at both ends and look at it for crushed spots. Then use the tools to split the problem in half. First, plug the loopback plug into the PC's network port. If the link light comes on or the port's self-test passes, the NIC is working, so the fault is outside the PC. If it fails, the NIC itself is the suspect. Next, disconnect the patch cable and connect each end to a piece of the cable tester. If every wire tests good, the cable is fine, so your next theory moves to the wall jack or the switch port it feeds. If a wire shows as open (broken) or miswired, the cable is confirmed as the cause. If a theory is ruled out, set a new one or escalate. Do not keep guessing.

Plan: replace the damaged patch cable with a known-good cable of a suitable length. First consider any impact. Here, Dana is already offline, so the change carries little risk, but you should tell her what you are doing. Implement: connect the new cable from the PC to the wall jack. Route it along the desk edge or under a cable cover, not across the floor under the chair wheels. This preventive step stops the new cable from being crushed again. Verify full system functionality, not just one sign of progress. Check that the link light is on. Run ipconfig and confirm the PC now has a normal address from DHCP, not a 169.254 address. Then confirm Dana can open the shared drive and a website. Finally, ask Dana to confirm everything she needs works. A common mistake is to stop as soon as the link light comes on, without confirming that the PC got a real address and that the user's actual tasks work.

The ticket should record the original symptoms: no network access, link light off, and a 169.254 APIPA address. It should note the key clue, the weekend desk move. It should list each theory and test with its result, for example: loopback test passed, so the NIC is fine; cable tester showed a broken wire. Then record the fix (cable replaced and rerouted away from the chair), how you verified it (DHCP address received, shared drive and web access confirmed by the user), and the outcome and date. Skipping documentation means the next technician has no history to work from. They may repeat the same tests and waste time. The pattern also goes unnoticed: here, the lesson is that office moves can damage cables, so future moves should include checking and routing cables. Good notes also build a knowledge base that speeds up similar fixes later.
